docs.title: The Kurt Programming Language Reference
docs.text:
Author: Stefan Harmeling (implementation); this reference rewritten 2026-09-04 to match the current behaviour of src/kurt/kurt.py.

This is a reference for the current behaviour of Kurt: what each keyword does, what the grammar allows, and what is and isn't checked. It describes things as they are, not as they're planned to become — see dev-notes.md for the history of why things ended up this way. The logic itself -- which symbols are variables, when a line follows, what a block proves, what crosses a file boundary, who may postulate -- is specified in kurt-spec.md, short and normative. To actually learn Kurt hands-on, start with keywords/00-true.kurt and work through the numbered lessons instead; this document is for looking things up once you already know roughly what you're looking for.

Every claim below was checked against the interpreter while writing this document (kurt <file>.kurt, or kurt interactively), not just read out of the source.

This site is generated from doc/kurt-ref.md of Kurt 0.12.0. Try Kurt in the browser: the playground.

docs.title: 9. Blocks and natural deduction
docs.text:
Every open proof/assume/case/let/pick/sandbox/expect pushes a new level onto the knowledge base. summary prints where the proof is: the open blocks with what opened them (; open: case A), the claims of open shows still to prove, the latest facts, and what could come next -- the same view that breakpoint and kurt -i show after stopping (§10), and that the playground and the editors use. list has a different job: it inspects declarations and facts retained from loaded theories. A block's own const/var declarations and any axioms used inside it disappear again once the block closes; only the formula the block's closing produces survives, on the parent level.

Indentation drives block closing, identically whether you're reading a file or typing/pasting into the interactive shell. Dedenting — writing (or, in the shell, typing) a line less indented than the block's content — closes as many levels as the drop in indentation implies, applying whatever each level's closing rule is (impl-intro, forall-intro, ..., below). There is no separate "shell mode" for this: the interactive shell reads real leading whitespace exactly like a file does, so pasting file content into kurt -i behaves the same as running it as a file. To help with typing, the shell (at a terminal) starts each line with the indentation of the current block, one level (four spaces) deeper after a line that opens a block; a backspace over the indentation dedents by one level. The shell edits its lines itself, the same on macOS, Linux and Windows (no readline): ←/→, Home/End, Delete, Ctrl-A/E/K/U/W, the history with ↑/↓ (kept in ~/.kurt_history), Ctrl-R to search it, Tab (below), Ctrl-C drops the line, Ctrl-D on an empty line ends the shell; a long line wraps, and pasted lines are read one after the other. Not at a terminal (a pipe), it reads plain lines. Two keywords remain as optional alternatives to dedenting, and work identically in files and the shell: qed (§7 — still needs a real dedent, but also checks you're closing a proof) and break (§9.5 — needs no dedent at all, and is the only way to close a sandbox other than dedenting past it).

Running a file itself already starts one level deep, inside an implicit sandbox (the same mechanism load uses, see §8.2); summary doesn't list that one.

docs.title: 9.1 assume and case
docs.text:
assume EXPR
    ...
(closes by dedenting, or `qed`/`break`)

Opens a block that adds EXPR as a local axiom; for a conjunction A ∧ B, its parts are facts too, shown as derived lines 6a A, 6b B ("and-elim"; also for case and pick ... with A ∧ B). Closing it derives "impl-intro": whatever you proved last inside the block becomes EXPR implies <that>, on the parent level. If the last thing derived inside the block was literally false, closing additionally derives not EXPR via "not-intro" (both formulas are added). Inside the block, the free variables of EXPR are fixed: in assume P $x, $x is one arbitrary object, the same in every line of the block -- so P $x follows, but not P $y. Closing the block generalizes again: P $x implies ... holds for every $x. case closes like assume: a sequence of cases produces one EXPR implies <goal> for every branch. On the final explicit goal, Kurt looks for a flat or fact and exactly one such implication for every alternative. This shortcut is available only when the theory contains the general binary or-elim schema; it does not assign a built-in meaning to an operator merely named or. A dedicated case-elim certificate records that rule and the finite list, and the independent kernel checks both. This works for any number of alternatives without generating a schematic n-premise rule or searching a Cartesian product of facts. The disjunction itself must already be derivable/used, and every branch must have the same goal. Forgetting a branch, the disjunction fact, or the final explicit claim is the most common way a case proof silently doesn't finish — it fails with an ordinary "can not derive" on that final line, not a case-specific error.

The running time of case (measured with scripts/bench_case.py, 2026-10-09, see dev/lab-notes.md): the final case-elim step itself is cheap and grows about quadratically with the number n of alternatives -- about 50 ms for n = 128 -- and it is always case-elim, never a combination the general search finds. The blocks are ordinary lines, though: if every block derives the goal with one of n rules that all have the goal as their conclusion, each block's search tries all of them, and the whole proof grows about cubically (about 0.2 s for n = 16, 5 s for n = 64, 40 s for n = 128 on a slow machine). For proofs with a handful of cases this doesn't matter. For very many cases, implications that name their case (A3 implies G, stated or proven) are fast: then case-elim uses them directly, without blocks (0.4 s for n = 128).

docs.title: 9.2 let
docs.text:
let SYMBOL             ; or a comma-separated list: let x, y, z
let CONDITION           ; e.g. let x>0
let SYMBOL with CONDITION   ; the same, naming the constant, e.g. let x with P(x)
    ...

Introduces one or more brand-new constants (each must not already be a declared constant, nor fixed by an enclosing assume; a $ or % name is refused: the free $-variables of a claim need no let, they are one arbitrary object in its proof). A condition (let x>0) also uses the condition as a local axiom, in one step. Closing the block derives "forall-intro": the last thing proven inside becomes universally quantified over each new constant, in reverse declaration order, skipping any that turn out to be statement variables. let x with C is let C, with the constant named: it is rejected if C is about another symbol.

let and pick take their conditions the same way, but they are opposite rules: let assumes the condition for an arbitrary x and gives "for all x" (∀-introduction); pick needs a known ∃ and gives a witness (∃-elimination). A pick without a matching ∃ says so, and suggests let.

docs.title: 9.3 pick
docs.text:
pick SYMBOL with FACT
pick FACT              ; the same, with the SYMBOL that FACT is about, e.g. pick c > 0
    ...

Requires some already-known formula exists $x P in the theory such that substituting the new SYMBOL for $x in P gives exactly FACT -- or one that follows in one step, which Kurt then shows as a derived line 13a before the pick (e.g. from P(c) and a rule P($x) ⇒ ∃ y (Q y), pick b with Q(b) derives ∃ b (Q b) first). If found, it opens a block with SYMBOL as a new constant and FACT as a local axiom. Closing the block derives "exists-elim": the last formula proven inside must not mention SYMBOL (checked, and also not mention any other constant introduced on the block's own level) — with that check passed, it becomes the block's result on the parent level, without any reference to the witness.

From an existential with a condition, exists $x > 0 P($x) (§4.4), FACT is the condition and the body for the witness: pick c with c > 0 ∧ P c -- as logic.kurt's "exists-cond-def" says, ∃ (sub $x $v %C) %P is ∃ $w ((sub $x $w %C) ∧ (sub $v $w %P)), so no detour through that rule is needed.

Several witnesses at once: pick x, y, z with F is pick x with ∃ y ∃ z F, pick y with ∃ z F and pick z with F, one inside the other -- three blocks, but the lines indent once, and a dedent closes all three (the existential ∃ x ∃ y ∃ z F, or one step to it, must be known). The names are distinct, and only the last carries with F. A break gives up all the blocks the pick line opened (they share one indentation), not only the innermost.

The formula side has the same list: ∃ x, y, z P is ∃ x ∃ y ∃ z P, and ∀ x, y P is ∀ x ∀ y P (the parser writes the binder once for each name, for the binders that are nested, §4.4; proofs/debug/exists-several-variables.kurt). Each name can have its own condition, ∀ x > 0, y > 0 P (∀ x > 0 ∀ y > 0 P); a condition after a list of plain names belongs to one variable, so ∃ x, y > 0 P is a ParseError (write ∃ x, y > 0 P as ∃ x > 0, y > 0 P or ∃ x ∃ y > 0 P). Only the two quantifiers take a list, not sum, lim, ... (their body or range is not repeatable).

SYMBOL must be a bare new-or-existing name, unlike let's otherwise similar let SYMBOL / let SYMBOL>0 (§9.2) — a picked witness can never carry an extra condition of its own the way a let-bound one can: let's condition becomes an assumption that gets quantified away when the block closes, but a picked witness is existential, so an unearned extra condition on it would just be an unproven fact about a specific value, not a sound derivation. pick x>0 with FACT is therefore rejected outright (EvalError) rather than silently accepted or silently ignored; the witness's only property comes from FACT itself. Without with, as in pick c > 0, the whole line is the FACT (as let c > 0 is the condition), and the witness is the one new symbol it is about.

docs.title: 9.4 sandbox
docs.text:
sandbox
    ...
(closes by dedenting, discarding everything inside -- or by `break`, immediately)

A scratch block: everything inside is discarded by default, never merged into the surrounding theory, whether it closes by dedenting (§9's introduction) or by break (§9.5) right away. The end of the file closes a sandbox still open there like a dedent, discarding its content (sandbox ; 5 closed, its content is discarded).

docs.title: 9.5 break
docs.text:
break     ; discard the current block immediately, without proving anything

break closes the current block right away, discarding it — no impl-intro, forall-intro, etc., nothing is added anywhere — without needing to dedent past it first. Works identically in a file or the interactive shell, and on any open block: it gives up the innermost open thing. Breaking out of a proof gives up only that attempt: the show it was trying to prove stays open, and a new proof can follow. Right after a show, or after the break of its proof, no block is open for the claim, so break withdraws the claim itself — break, break gives up a proof completely. A withdrawn claim is still to do: the file ends with "Proof almost checked" and the claim among its todos (it is not complete, for --json and the grader). A claim that is neither proved nor withdrawn is an error at the end of the file ("has no proof"). (Before 0.9, the first break withdrew the claim too.)

break can't close the file's own implicit top-level scope (§8.2, §9's introduction) — there is no real, user-written block there to close, so it raises a clean error rather than doing anything to it.

docs.title: 9.6 expect
docs.text:
expect "KIND"
    ...
expect "KIND" "TEXT"
    ...

Opens a block whose content is expected to raise an error of the given KIND (and, with TEXT, whose message contains TEXT). The kinds, each for one stage of reading and checking a line:

kind when ScanError a symbol can't be scanned (an unknown character, a number with too many digits) ParseError the line can't be read: brackets, indentation, a chain's continuation, an incomplete expression EvalError the line is readable, but the statement isn't allowed: wrong arguments of a keyword, conflicting declarations, load problems, a claim that isn't a statement TypeError sorts, the arguments of sub, the variable or condition of a binder ProofError a claim can't be derived, a block can't close as it should

(Every KurtException carries its .kind, see KurtException.KNOWN_KINDS in kurt.py.) If something inside the block raises exactly that kind, the whole block (including anything it did) is discarded and checking simply continues with the next statement, the same way break discards a sandbox. If the block closes normally with nothing having raised, that itself is now the failure (ExpectationError: this `expect "KIND"` block finished without raising a `KIND`); if something raises but of the wrong kind, that's also a failure, reported with both kinds shown.

This exists so a proof file (or a lesson, see keywords/16-expect.kurt) can demonstrate a mistake and have Kurt itself confirm it still fails the expected way, rather than relying on a comment nobody re-checks, or on a separate test harness matching exact (and therefore fragile — see dev/todo-claude.md, in git history) error text.

The expected error may come from anywhere inside the block: from a statement directly inside it, from inside a nested block (assume, proof, another expect, ...), or while such a nested block closes (a failing qed, or the dedent that closes a let/pick/proof). In the last case the line that triggered the dedent is already outside the expect block, so it is still evaluated afterwards. Any lines of the block after the one that raised the error are skipped. Since the content of an expect block is always discarded, use is allowed inside it (see §6.2). A second string is a text that the error message must contain: expect "ProofError" "can not derive" (a string can't contain "). A break inside expect closes the expect block itself; an error that only a whole file can make (a proof still unfinished at its end, a show without a proof, break at its top level, ...) is checked by expect around a load of such a file (see tests/how-to-write-test-proofs.md).

docs.title: 4. Building the grammar
docs.text: Kurt's grammar is not fixed — the fixity, precedence, and arity of every operator (including implies/and/space itself) is declared from Kurt source, using a small set of keywords, and looked up dynamically by the parser (a Pratt/TDOP parser). This is what "extensible from Kurt source" means throughout CLAUDE.md.

docs.title: 4.1 infix, prefix, postfix
docs.text:
infix OP lbp rbp     ; e.g. infix "+" 20 20
prefix OP rbp        ; e.g. prefix "-" 100
postfix OP lbp       ; e.g. postfix "!" 100

Each accepts a comma-separated list to declare several operators in one line (e.g. infix "+" 20 20, "-" 20 20). Binding powers control precedence and associativity: for infix, lbp > rbp makes the operator right- associative (as implies is: infix implies 13 12, so A implies B implies C parses as A implies (B implies C); and number.kurt's infix ^ 75 74, so 2 ^ 3 ^ 2 is 2 ^ 9); lbp == rbp (as with + above) makes it left-associative (a - b - c is (a - b) - c), and a flat operator (§4.5) collects all its arguments anyway. Declaring the same symbol both infix and prefix is allowed (useful for something like unary/binary -); declaring it as more than one of infix/prefix/postfix/a bracket otherwise is an error. Fixity alone does not classify a symbol as constant or variable.

Called with no arguments (infix, prefix, postfix), each prints every currently-declared operator of that kind, across all open levels. The other property keywords (const, var, sort, prop, arity, brackets, binder, chain, flat, sym, and alias) work the same way. Every listed entry's comment gives both its scope level and the source location that established that exact property, for example ; level 1, natural.kurt:20. A basename is shown normally; if two loaded files have the same basename, Kurt shows their paths to keep the locations unambiguous. Hard-coded core declarations have no source line and therefore show only their level.

docs.title: 4.2 brackets
docs.text:
brackets LEFT RIGHT     ; e.g. brackets "[" "]"

Declares a new matching pair of bracket symbols. Only Kurt's own ( ) pair (declared exactly this way in minimal.kurt) is treated as pure, disappearing grouping — (A) really is just A. Any other bracket pair you declare yourself stays around as a genuine operator: [A] parses to a real term whose operator is an internal name combining [ and ] (rendered as [] if you parse/format sexpr it), not to A. Custom brackets are meant to carry their own meaning (e.g. ⟨a, b⟩ for a scalar product, brackets ⟨ ⟩; in the shell \langle, \rangle) via arity/prop/use axioms about the resulting operator, not as alternative parentheses. brackets takes exactly the two symbols — there is no separate binding-power argument. The two delimiter symbols become constants. A later prop LEFT ... or builtin LEFT ... declaration applies to the combined bracket expression, and listings print the source left delimiter rather than its internal combined name.

docs.title: 4.3 arity
docs.text:
arity SYMBOL N         ; e.g. arity f 2:         f a b
arity SYMBOL SHAPE     ; e.g. arity g (_, _):    g(a, b), one argument, a pair
                       ;      arity sum _ (_, _) _:  sum i (0, n) f

Declares that SYMBOL is a plain (non-infix/prefix/postfix) function or predicate symbol taking exactly N arguments by space-application: f a b parses as one call (f a b). The shape says more, written as the symbol is used: _ for an argument, (_, _) for a tuple of two (also nested, ((_, _), _)); Kurt checks each use, so g(a) or g(a, b, c) with arity g (_, _) is an error ("g takes g (_, _)"), and a variable may stand for a tuple (g($p)). A symbol with no declared arity defaults to arity 0: it takes all the arguments that follow it, curried, and nothing checks them (§3.1). You cannot set an arity on a symbol that's already infix/prefix/postfix or a bracket (their arities — 2, 1, 1 — are implicit and fixed), and you cannot re-set an arity once declared.

Round brackets group, so f(x) is f x, ((a)) is a, and f(x) = x * x reads as usual. Round brackets around a list are a tuple, a term of its own (since 0.9): (a, b) is a pair, (a, b, c) a triple, and (a, (b, c)) a pair whose second component is a pair -- so g(a, b) is g applied to one argument, the pair, never g a b (before 0.9: g a b for a g of arity 2). a, b, c without round brackets is a list: the elements in {a, b} or ⟨a, b⟩, or the formulas of use A, B; {(a, b)} is the set with one element, the pair. Binders (sum, ∀, ...) take their arguments as written, e.g. sum i (0, n) f with the pair (0, n).

def defines a function of a tuple by its components, def f($x, $y) = ...: tuples are free, two are equal only if their components are, so this is conservative (doc/kurt-soundness.md §8.14).

An operator alone in round brackets is the operator itself -- as the argument of an operator parameter, group(G, (∘), e, inv), group(R, (+), 0, (-)); (- x) is still - x. An operator is no object (§5.3): elsewhere, (+) or a bare f is a type error. An operator can also be a variable -- var ∘ and infix ∘ 70 70 -- then $a ∘ $b in a rule matches x + y as well as a ∘ b (by the rules of the operator it stands for, e.g. flat, sym). See §5.4 and group.kurt.

A relation as a parameter works the same way: a variable with a statement as its result, var R and prop R 0, then R(x, y) -- or with infix R 20 20 also x R y, which matches x < y or x ∈ y -- e.g. def reflexive((R), $A) ⇔ ∀ x ∈ $A (x R x), and then reflexive((<=), A). ($R(x, y) is a term, not a formula: a $ variable stands for a term.) The symbols ~, ∼ (\sim), ≈ (\approx), ≺ (\prec), ≼ (\preceq) are free for relations of your own. Names may end in primes, a', f'', and a Greek letter may have digits, λ1.

Empty brackets ((), {}, ...) are allowed and parse to nothing; the only place this is meaningful is directly after an arity-0 symbol, where f() then parses to exactly f — the same expression as writing f alone, matching ordinary mathematical usage of () for "no arguments." Directly after a symbol with a declared arity of 1 or more, f() is instead a clear, specific EvalError ("empty brackets () cannot supply an argument for f, which needs N argument(s)"), not a confusing parse — empty parens can never actually supply a real argument.

docs.title: 4.4 binder
docs.text:
binder SYMBOL            ; e.g. binder forall
binder SYMBOL POWER      ; e.g. binder sum 65: the binding power of the body (below)
nested SYMBOL, ...       ; e.g. nested forall, exists: the variable may be a list (below)

Declares SYMBOL a variable-binding operator: its first argument is treated as a bound variable (or, with the sugar below, a condition, a statement whose free variable is the one being bound) for the rest of the expression. forall/exists are declared exactly this way, in logic.kurt (arity forall 2, exists 2, binder forall, exists), together with their roles (builtin forall universal, ..., §8.1) and their axioms (forall-elim, exists-intro). For a plain space-applied binder, the symbol must already have an arity of at least 2 (the bound variable plus at least one more argument). An infix operator may instead be a binder, as set-builder | is: its left operand contains the condition and its right operand is the body. A binder cannot also be prefix, flat, sym, chained, calculator-bound, variable, or already used in a formula. binder gives a fixed scope rule, so it makes the symbol a constant and reports const SYMBOL ; added constant when that role was not already explicit.

The body of a binder, and its power. Without a power, the body is one tight argument, as f x takes its argument: sum i (1, n) i * 2 is (sum i (1, n) i) * 2, and P x > 0 is (P x) > 0. With one, binder sum 65, the body is read with that binding power (a number from 1 to 89; the operators that bind tighter than it are inside the body, the others outside): sum i (1, n) i * 2 is sum i (1, n) (i * 2) (* is 70, + is 60: sum i (1, n) i + 1 is (sum i (1, n) i) + 1). A body that is an application is whole, ∀ x P x ∧ Q is (∀ x (P x)) ∧ Q. Parenthesized bodies read the same either way, and what Kurt prints is parenthesized. The power belongs to the binder and goes with it through load (two files must declare the same one). It is for a binder with a space, not for an infix one. The theories use it: logic.kurt gives forall, exists, existsunique the power 17 (comparisons, arithmetic and not inside the body, and, or, implies, iff outside: ∀ x x > 0 ∧ x < 5 is (∀ x (x > 0)) ∧ x < 5), and analysis.kurt and integral.kurt give sum, max, min, argmax, argmin, sup, inf, lim, integral, integrable the power 65 (* and / inside, + and - outside: sum i (1, n) i * 2 + 1 is (sum i (1, n) (i * 2)) + 1).

Several variables. nested forall, exists (logic.kurt) says that the variable of these binders may be a list: ∀ x, y P is ∀ x ∀ y P, and each name can have its own condition, ∀ x > 0, y > 0 P (∀ x > 0 ∀ y > 0 P); a condition after a list of plain names, ∃ x, y > 0 P, is a ParseError. Only a binder of two arguments (the variable and the body) can be nested, not sum or lim.

The scope of the bound variable is the condition and the last argument, the body; arguments in between are outside of it, as in mathematics: in sum i (a, b) T the range (a, b), in lim v a T the point a. So in sum x (0, n) (sum x (0, x) x), the inner range (0, x) is the outer x.

A schema variable in the body of a binder normally stands for something that does not depend on the bound variable — in (∀ $x ($x = $T)), $T is one fixed term. A statement variable %A may depend on it (that's what "forall-elim" is about), and so may a term variable $T of an axiom that occurs as the whole body of a binder over the same variable, and otherwise only inside binders over it or as the body of a sub for it, as in the sum axioms (sum $i ($a, $a) $T) = sub $i $a $T and (sum $i ($a, $b+1) $T) = (sub $i ($b+1) $T) + (sum $i ($a, $b) $T) (see analysis.kurt) — such a $T stands for any summand, which the axioms only ever use for the bound $i or with something substituted for it — or in the sum rule of derivatives, (diff $v $a $S) ∧ (diff $v $a $T) ⇒ (deriv $v $a ($S + $T)) = ... (derivative.kurt). Only an axiom (use, def, todo) is read like this, and not the variables of the ∀s it writes out: a proven fact holds for every term in place of its variables (a proof with let c is about terms c). This is decided by the form of the rule alone: there is no way to declare a dependence ($T[$i], as in Isabelle) or a distinct-variable condition ("$x doesn't occur in $T", as in Metamath) -- a decision (2026-10-06): the form shows where a dependence is meant, the kernel checks it, and no theory has needed more. Anywhere else, $T can't depend on the bound variable, and a rule that would need it can't be written.

Conditions. The "bound variable" position may instead be a condition on it: ∀ $n ∈ Nat P($n), ∃ $d > 0 ..., lim $x > 0 0 (f $x). Unbracketed, it is a relation whose left-hand side is the variable; its right-hand side extends over infix operators (∀ $x ∈ A ∪ B ...) but stops at the first function application, which is where the body starts -- except for f(x) written without a space, which stays in the condition (∀ $x ∈ Perp(M) ...). In parentheses, any condition works, ∀ ($x > 0 ∧ $x < 1) (P $x). Which variable is bound: the first symbol of the condition, in the order it is written, that is new or a variable and not bound by an enclosing binder -- constants, predicates and operators are skipped. So ∀ x ∈ M ... binds a new x (also a plain name outside of a block), ∀ ($a ∈ $G) ... in a rule binds $a, ∀ ($x < $y) ... binds $x, ∀ c < x ... with a constant c binds x, ∀ (P $x) ... with a predicate P binds $x, and in ∀ (0 < e) (∀ (e < x) ...) the inner binder binds x (e is bound outside). Kurt decides this when it reads the line, before anything is reordered (a sym operator sorts its arguments), and stores the variable with the condition: the binder binds the same variable whenever the formula is used later, whatever is a constant then (when a block closes, its constants are free again -- this used to change the reading, and Kurt refused such a block). A printed formula reads back the same way. A condition without such a symbol is an error ("has no variable to bind").

A condition is part of the formula: ∀ $x > 0 P($x) is not the same formula as ∀ $x ($x > 0 ⇒ P($x)), and the engine doesn't treat it as an implication. What a condition means is said by rules, like for any other operator — for ∀ and ∃ in logic.kurt:

use (∀ (sub $x $v %C) %P) ∧ (sub $x $a %C)  ⇒  sub $v $a %P                     "forall-cond-elim"
use (sub $x $a %C) ∧ (sub $v $a %P)  ⇒  ∃ (sub $x $v %C) %P                     "exists-cond-intro"
use (∀ (sub $x $v %C) %P)  ⇔  ∀ $w ((sub $x $w %C) ⇒ (sub $v $w %P))           "forall-cond-def"
use (∃ (sub $x $v %C) %P)  ⇔  ∃ $w ((sub $x $w %C) ∧ (sub $v $w %P))           "exists-cond-def"

In a rule (use/def), a binder sub $x $v %C stands for any condition: $v is the bound variable, and %C the condition with the hole $x for it — matching ∀ ($y > 0) ... gives %C = $x > 0, with every occurrence of the bound variable in the hole. So %C never mentions the bound variable itself, and %C may only be used with something substituted for $x, as sub $x ... %C (checked when the rule is stated). A binder with a condition never matches one without, so rules for both kinds are written separately (see lim in analysis.kurt).

So from ∀ $x > 0 P($x) and 1 > 0 follows P 1 in one step ("forall-cond-elim"), while ∀ $x ($x > 0 ⇒ P($x)) takes a step of its own ("forall-cond-def") — e.g. to close ∀ $c ($c ∈ A ⇒ $c ∈ B) (the definition of A ⊂ B) after a let x ∈ A block, which gives ∀ x ∈ A (x ∈ B).

Several quantifiers with conditions. A step is one application of one rule, and a fact with conditions on two quantifiers, ∀ x ∈ V ∀ y ∈ V ((x - y) = (2 * x - (x + y))), takes one "forall-cond-elim" per ∀. Kurt does it for you when the line doesn't follow in one step: with a ∈ V and b ∈ V known, the line a - b = 2 * a - (a + b) is checked with an extra step of its own, the instance for the first ∀, shown before it:

   ∀ (y ∈ V) ((a - y) = (2 * a - (a + y)))   ; 9a by forall-cond-elim(V2, 7)
9  (a - b) = (2 * a - (a + b))               ; by forall-cond-elim(9a, 8)

Two or three conditioned quantifiers are handled, and a condition may mention the variable before it (∀ x ∈ V ∀ y > x ...). If a condition is not known, the line fails as before, and the message names it: "V2 (line 4) has 2 quantifiers with conditions: it gives this line by 2 "forall-cond-elim" steps, but b ∈ V is not known". The same fact without conditions, ∀ x ∀ y ..., is stripped into variables and is one step. (Each step has its certificate, the kernel is unchanged; doc/kurt-soundness.md §8.52.)

Unique existence. logic.kurt declares the binder existsunique, written ∃! x P(x) (∃! is one symbol; in the shell \exists!). Its meaning is its definition, "existsunique-def": ∃! x P(x) iff ∃ x (P(x) ∧ ∀ y (P(y) ⇒ y = x)); with a condition, ∃! x ∈ M P(x) is ∃! x (x ∈ M ∧ P(x)) ("existsunique-cond-def"). Three rules follow from the definition and save the steps through it: "existsunique-intro" (from P(a) and ∀ y (P(y) ⇒ y = a)), "existsunique-exists" (∃! gives ∃), and "existsunique-unique" (from ∃! x P(x), P(a) and P(b) follows a = b). They are axioms, since a general proof would need sub in its lines; proofs/natural-deduction/ existsunique.kurt derives each of them from the definition alone, for a predicate P. To use the witness, get ∃ x P(x) and pick from it, or unfold the definition.

docs.title: 4.5 flat and sym
docs.text:
flat OP     ; e.g. flat "+"
sym OP      ; e.g. sym "+"

Both require OP to already be infix. They are two separate laws, and each can be declared without the other: flat is associativity, sym commutativity; the normal form of a term and the search use each on its own. flat OP means a run of OP doesn't nest two arguments at a time in the parsed term — a + b + c parses to a single (+ a b c) rather than (+ (+ a b) c) (compare parse a + b + c before and after declaring flat), and so do (a + b) + c and a + (b + c): they are the same term, and the order of the arguments stays as written. sym OP means OP's arguments may be reordered when Kurt searches the theory for a match — an axiom about a + b also matches a goal written as b + a. An operator that is both flat and sym (like and/or) gets its arguments canonically sorted before matching, which means Kurt effectively does multiset matching on it: A and B and C matches a stored C and A and B directly, not just pairwise swaps.

flat alone is the law of an associative operation that isn't commutative, the product of a group or of matrices (flat +, times and sym + in matrix.kurt and field.kurt). From P((a ∘ b) ∘ c) with only flat ∘, Kurt gets P(a ∘ (b ∘ c)) (the same term a ∘ b ∘ c), but not P(c ∘ b ∘ a) or P(b ∘ a ∘ c); with only sym ∘, it gets P(c ∘ (b ∘ a)) (each ∘ swapped), but not P(a ∘ (b ∘ c)); with both, every order and grouping. (A flat operator is a constant, see below: group.kurt's ∘, a variable for any group's operation, has its associativity in the definition of a group, associative($G, (∘)), instead.) Each of flat/sym can only be declared once per operator (redeclaring raises an error), and if the operator already has a partial prop signature (§5), that signature must be consistent with binary use (both argument positions statement places, or neither; no signature information beyond position 2).

Declaring flat or sym is a claim (associativity, commutativity), so it must come before the operator is used in any formula, and it can't be made for an operator that comes with one of Kurt's theories or its core (e.g. sym - or sym implies is an error) — see "frozen operators" in §8.2. It also fixes the operator's meaning, so either declaration makes it a constant. A flat operator cannot share its symbol with a prefix form (flattening would erase the distinction between unary and binary trees); neither property can be attached to a binding or variable operator.

docs.title: 4.6 chain
docs.text:
chain OP1 OP2 ...     ; e.g. chain = <=  or  chain iff implies

Chains of relations, in one place: a < b < c on one line is read as a < b and b < c (below, for every relation between terms, prop OP 0, declared in a chain or not), and the chain line, by the order of its relations, gives the transitivity facts, so a < c follows from it in one step (with number.kurt's chain = <= <: "chain-trans-2-2"); a chain can also go on over indented continuation lines. chain declares that the listed infix operators may be written one after another across indented continuation lines, mimicking how mathematicians chain (in)equalities: after a chain is declared, writing

x = y
  < z

is sugar for two separate checked lines, x = y and x < z (the second line's left-hand side is filled in from the previous line's right-hand side, and the operator used is the strongest one seen so far in the chain, by index in the declared list — this is why chain = < lets = , <-chains resolve to < once a < has appeared).

A term on a line of its own. The usual way to write an equation in two lines starts with the left side alone:

(a + b) * c
  = a * c + b * c

A line that is a term (no statement) waits for the next line: if that is indented deeper and starts with a relation of a chain, the two are the statement (a + b) * c = a * c + b * c, checked as one line (its output is at the line of the relation), and further lines = ... go on as above. Only the relations of a chain continue a term, so - x after a term is no continuation. Otherwise (the next line is not indented, starts with anything else, a block keyword, or the file ends) the term line is the error it always was, "must be a statement", at the line of the term. The shell waits the same way, so a file can be pasted into it; typing a term and then something else shows the error at that next line. Blank lines and comments between the two lines don't matter.

Declaring a chain also generates real, directly usable transitivity axioms — one for every ordered pair of the chain's operators, using the same "pick the operator with the larger index" rule as the parsing sugar above. For chain = <= <, that includes the familiar $a < $b and $b < $c implies $a < $c, but also every mixed pair like $a <= $b and $b < $c implies $a < $c. They are named "chain-trans-I-J", by the positions of the two relations in the chain (counted from 0): < with < is "chain-trans-2-2", = with < is "chain-trans-0-2". So given x = y and y < z as two separately-proven facts (not written as one continuation-line chain), x < z really is now a single derivation step, citing the auto-generated fact (the line's reason lists the facts in the order the search used them, not in the order of the chain) — you don't need to hand-write these per theory (number.kurt used to; it no longer does). This only combines two facts in one hop, the same as every other inference rule — three or more links in a chain of relations still need an explicit intermediate step, same as any other multi-hop reasoning (§6.1's single-hop limitation still applies beyond one combination).

Relations can also be chained on a single line: a = b <= c < d means a = b and b <= c and c < d, reusing each middle term. This applies to any infix operator with a statement as its result and no statements as arguments (prop OP 0, e.g. =, ≠, <, <=, in), whether or not it is declared in a chain — not to connectives like and, iff, implies. The operators of one chain must have the same binding power: with infix <= 50 50, < 50 50 and = at 20 20, a = b <= c < d is not a chain but a = ((c < d) and (b <= c)). Parentheses switch it off: (a = b) = c is still an equation between a = b and c. Since the auto-generated transitivity axioms take a conjunction as premise, a chain of two relations on one line like a = b <= c directly gives a <= c in one more step (proofs/arithmetic/chains.kurt); with three, a = b <= c < d, a <= c is not derivable in one step. A same-line chain can't (yet) be continued on indented lines below it.

Continuation lines must be indented relative to the line that starts the chain; writing the continuation at the same indentation is a ParseError, not a chain. All declared chains together must form a DAG (no operator ordering may create a cycle across different chain declarations) — this is checked when the chain is declared. Every member must be a constant, non-binding infix relation with a statement as its result. chain adds those const and prop OP 0 declarations when necessary and reports them explicitly; a variable operator cannot acquire the generated fixed transitivity rules.

A chain has at most three operators (at most 9 rules). With --strict (§1), outside the trusted theories, a chain generates nothing: each of its rules -- one for every ordered pair, ($a Ri $b) and ($b Rj $c) implies ($a Rk $c), the later relation absorbing the earlier, so chain = < is a different claim than chain < = -- must be a fact before the chain line, or follow in one step (checked as a line is: the search, then the kernel); a missing one is an error that lists the show lines to prove. The chain's notation (continuation lines, a ≺ b ≺ c) then uses the proved facts. Unproven, chain R for x R y meaning y = x + 1 would give 3 = 2.

docs.title: 4.7 alias
docs.text:
alias NEW OLD     ; e.g. alias "⇒" implies

alias gives an existing symbol an additional name, resolved in the scanner (i.e. before parsing, with no inference step) — implies and ⇒ are completely interchangeable everywhere, including inside axioms already stored in the theory. This is different from def (§6.2), which introduces a genuinely new constant that needs an inference step to unfold (equal-elim for def c = ...; a def P iff ... is used directly as an implication in both directions).

A declaration written with an alias is about its symbol: after alias ⊆ subset, tex ⊆ \subseteq or chain ⊆ declare tex/chain for subset (a declaration of the alias itself would never apply, since the scanner reads every ⊆ as subset).

The words of Kurt's theories. In the theories that come with Kurt (src/kurt/theories/), the standard name of every symbol is ASCII, a word, and the Unicode symbol is its alias: union and ∪, as implies and ⇒, forall and ∀, <= and ≤, Nat and ℕ (todo 61). A file may write either: A ∪ B and A union B are the same term, and a line is printed as it is written, with the symbols of the line (x ∈ (A ∪ B) or x in (A union B); the brackets and the order of the arguments of a sym operator are Kurt's, and that order follows the standard names). A line that Kurt derives keeps the symbols of the facts it comes from (a theory's rules are written with ∪); the listings and messages use the standard name: list, syntax, theory's declarations, an error message (`union`), a sort signature (set union 0 1 2). kurt --latex writes a word as its symbol (union is \cup, like ∪), and kurt --lean names a symbol without a lean declaration by its word (subset, divides, times_d2). Other files are free to declare Unicode symbols as they like; but the words are symbols of the theories now, so a file that loads set.kurt can't declare a union of its own (a symbol is declared by one file only, §8.2).

theory word symbol theory word symbol set.kurt in ∈ (and :) equality.kurt neq ≠ set.kurt subset ⊂ natural.kurt divides ∣ set.kurt superset ⊃ field.kurt, matrix.kurt times · set.kurt notin ∉ group.kurt compose ∘ set.kurt union ∪ lambda.kurt lambda λ set.kurt intersect ∩ lambda.kurt reduces ↦ set.kurt emptyset ∅ (and {}) lambda.kurt steps ⇝ set.kurt cross × lambda.kurt, modal.kurt proves ⊢ set.kurt to → modal.kurt imp, equiv →, ⇔ propositional.kurt true, false ⊤, ⊥ modal.kurt wedge, vee, neg ∧, ∨, ¬ propositional.kurt implies, invimplies, iff ⇒, ⇐, ⇔ (and ≡) modal.kurt bot ⊥ propositional.kurt and, or, not ∧, ∨, ¬ modal.kurt box, diamond □, ◇ logic.kurt forall, exists, existsunique ∀, ∃, ∃! number.kurt <=, >= ≤, ≥ natural.kurt Nat ℕ number.kurt Real, Int, Rat ℝ, ℤ, ℚ complex.kurt Complex ℂ finite.kurt setminus ∖

modal.kurt's connectives are those of its formulas (terms), not the core's implies, and, ...: hence imp, wedge, vee, neg, bot (conj would be complex.kurt's conjugate); ∅ is emptyset, since empty is the empty context of lambda.kurt and modal.kurt. A Greek letter that is a name stays one (group.kurt's inverse ι, an operator variable); λ, a binder, has a word.

docs.title: 4.8 Inspecting the grammar
docs.text: syntax (with no argument) prints every declared piece of syntax at every open level; syntax SYMBOL prints just what's known about one symbol. For the facts that mention a symbol too, not just its declarations, see info (§4.9). parse EXPR parses EXPR without checking it and prints both its s-expression form -- in the normal form Kurt stores and matches (flat operators flattened, the arguments of sym ones sorted: parse c + 1 + c gives (+ 1 c c); the exception is = and iff, which are sym for the search but keep their written order: parse b = a gives (= b a)) -- and the same per-symbol syntax info as syntax. tokenize EXPR shows the raw token stream before parsing. Each of infix/prefix/postfix/brackets/arity/binder/flat/sym/ chain/sort/prop/var/const/alias, called with no arguments, also prints its own currently-declared table.

docs.title: 4.9 Inspecting loaded theories
docs.text:
list shows which theory files are loaded. list files is the explicit spelling of the same command. Give it a loaded theory's stem or filename to see all declarations and formulas retained from that source:

list
list files
list natural
list natural.kurt

A category before the optional source narrows the result:

list const                 ; every known constant
list const natural         ; constants originating in natural.kurt
list infix natural.kurt    ; infix declarations originating there
list theory natural        ; all retained formulas originating there
list use natural           ; retained axioms originating there
list def natural           ; retained definitions originating there
list syntax natural        ; every retained declaration originating there

The declaration categories are prefix, infix, postfix, brackets, arity, binder, flat, sym, sort, prop, chain, var, const, and alias. A declared sort name is also a category, so list term lambda shows the retained term signatures. After list, symbols and declarations are synonyms for syntax (list symbols natural). Locations in a source-filtered result refer to the original file and line.

A source without .kurt matches the stem of a loaded file; a name ending in .kurt matches its basename; and a path selects that file. If two loaded files have the same stem or basename, Kurt asks for a path. Category names are reserved after list, so a theory called const.kurt is selected with list const.kurt.

Loading retains a theory's exported declarations and labelled, non-local facts. Therefore list natural describes the part of natural.kurt present in the current knowledge base, rather than reproducing the source file. It cannot show local declarations, unlabelled facts, comments, or intermediate proof lines that were discarded during loading.

list's SOURCE is always a file. To ask about one symbol instead -- its declarations (syntax SYMBOL), its def if it has one, and every retained fact that mentions it, wherever it came from -- use info SYMBOL:

load number
calc on
def four = 2 + 2
four = 4
info four
; const four                                ; ...
; def four = (2 + 2)                        ; ...
; four = 4                                  ; ...

info never resolves its argument as a file (unlike list), so a symbol and a loaded file happening to share a name never conflict: info four always means the symbol, even with a loaded four.kurt in scope -- list four still means that file.

docs.title: 8. Building the theory: hard-coded core vs. loaded theories
8.1 What's hard-coded (needs no load)
docs.text:
A pristine session starts with minimal.kurt's worth of syntax (space, comma -- a, b, c is one list, and (a, b, c) in round brackets a triple (§4.3) --, ( ), implies, and, the constant true, the substitution operator sub — sub $x $a %A is "%A with $a substituted for $x", only allowed in use/def to write axiom schemas like "forall-elim" or "equal-elim", and not nested (a rule about two variables is applied twice, one variable at a time); where the search finds $a and %A for a given formula, the hole $x is a subexpression -- a statement or a term --, and an operator only if it yields a term: see "Where the hole of sub may be" below) already declared -- the quantifiers forall/exists come with load logic (see below) -- plus these rules implemented directly in Python (not as use axioms you could remove):

  • "top-intro" — the bare symbol true is always provable.
  • "impl-elim" (modus ponens) — given A and A implies B anywhere in the theory, B is derivable.
  • "and-intro" — given A and B separately provable, A and B is derivable (and, symmetrically, a claimed conjunction is split into its conjuncts and each is derived separately).
  • "not-intro", automatically, as a side effect of closing an assume block (see §9.1) whose last derived line is literally false — this one isn't reachable as a standalone rule outside of that block-closing moment.
  • an iff as an implication — a fact A iff B (e.g. from def P iff ...) is used directly as A implies B and as B implies A, without a rule -- for the symbol with the role equivalence (propositional.kurt's iff, see builtin, §10).
  • "case-elim" — closing the case blocks of a disjunction (§9.1) gives the goal; it is justified by propositional.kurt's "or-elim", for any number of alternatives.
  • "chain-trans-I-J" — the transitivity rules a chain declaration generates (§4.6).
  • "by calc" — with calc on, a claim that computes to true, or to a fact, follows by the built-in calculator (§10).
  • forall-elim, effectively for free (with load logic) — every formula ever added to the theory has any outer universal quantifier stripped and its bound variable replaced by a fresh, freely-unifiable internal variable (as if it had been written as a $-schema to begin with) — so use forall x (A x) already lets A a derive for a specific a, with no explicit forall-elim step needed. The same for "forall-intro" (closing a let block) and "exists-elim" (closing a pick block). logic.kurt's forall-elim axiom still exists for the same reason a hard-coded rule sometimes also has a use equivalent lying around: explicit intermediate steps, and cases this automatic stripping doesn't reach (a forall that isn't the outermost operator of a stored formula). Only a forall without a condition is stripped: ∀ $x > 0 P($x) stays as it is, and is used via logic.kurt's rules for conditions (§4.4).

Where the hole of sub may be. A rule like "equal-elim", ($a = $b) ∧ (sub $x $a %A) ⇒ (sub $x $b %A), rewrites a formula by cutting a hole $x into it. The hole is a part of the formula that is a term or a statement -- and an operator counts only when it is a term on its own. A function symbol is: f with arity f 1 is an object, which an equation can name. So f = g rewrites f a:

load equality
const f, g, a
arity f 1, g 1
prop R
arity R 1
use f = g
use R (f a)
R (g a)                     ; by equal-elim(6, 7) -- the hole is the operator `f`

An operator with a statement as its result is not: =, ∧, or a predicate P with prop P and arity P 1 is, on its own, neither a term nor a statement -- it becomes a statement only applied to its arguments. So the hole is never the = of c = c (doc/kurt-soundness.md §8.40: cut there, "iff-subst" had turned R ((¬¬(=)) c c) into R (c = c)), and a bare such operator where a statement is required is a type error -- also an equivalence of two predicates:

load propositional
prop P, Q
arity P 1, Q 1
use P ⇔ Q                   ; TypeError: arg number 1 of `iff` must be a statement, but `P` is
                            ; an operator without its arguments -- apply it to its 1 argument, e.g. `P a`

State it for the arguments instead: use ∀ x (P x ⇔ Q x) (with load logic), and P a gives Q a. A binder (∀, ∃) is no hole either. An operator variable (var ∘ with infix ∘) is a different thing: it matches an operator by itself, through the unifier (∘ := +), not as a hole.

The quantifiers are declared in logic.kurt, which gives them their roles (builtin forall universal, exists existential, §10): the engine strips, closes let with, and opens pick from, only the binders with these roles. So the core has no quantifiers: a file for propositional or modal logic doesn't need them, a deep embedding may use the words for something else, and without load logic, let (over terms) and pick say that they need it.

Notably, "and-elim" (splitting a proven A and B back into A) is not hard-coded — you either state the specific instance yourself as a use axiom, or load propositional for a general one. A general "restatement" schema (%A implies %A) and a general "impl-intro" schema ((%A implies %B) implies (%A implies %B)) are also not hard-coded, despite once being drafted as if they were: a bare A implies A with nothing else known does not derive from nothing. Prove a specific instance instead (show/proof/assume/qed), or note that plain "restating" an already-proven fact is covered anyway by "impl-elim"'s own premise-less- implication case.

minimal.kurt is the core itself: Kurt reads its declarations when it starts, before anything else, and freezes them (only the parse rule of local and the internal marker of bound variables are made in kurt.py). It is never loaded -- load minimal is an error ("is the core, which every file starts with"). It deliberately declares no aliases: propositional.kurt supplies ⊤, ⇒, ∧, ∨, and ¬, and logic.kurt supplies ∀ and ∃.

docs.title: 8.2 load and the theory library
docs.text:
load NAME               ; load "path/to/name.kurt"
load NAME1, NAME2, ...

load searches, in order: the loading file's own directory (or the current directory, from the CLI/shell), then any -p/--path directory given on the command line, then Kurt's own packaged theories (src/kurt/theories/). The .kurt extension is added automatically if missing. The packaged theories can't be shadowed: load propositional always loads Kurt's own propositional.kurt, and a file propositional.kurt found earlier on the search path is an error (rename it) — def, and the checks built on the packaged theories, rely on their exact content. (A name with a directory, load ./propositional or load lib/propositional, is your own file, as written — not trusted, so under --strict it may not use anything.)

The symbols declared by a trusted theory file — one that comes with Kurt, or one found via -p DIR — are frozen: no other file can declare them flat or sym, or put them into a chain in a way that derives something new about them. E.g. chain ≠ (which would make ≠ transitive) is rejected, while chain = lt for a file's own relation lt is fine: a frozen operator may be combined with the file's own operators if the frozen ones come first (the chain's conclusions use the later operator) and are already chained that way in their theory. A file that has already finished loading is not loaded again (tracked via get_load_level, per level, inherited from parent levels) — so load propositional twice in a row, or from two different files that both depend on it, is a harmless no-op (logged as already loaded, skipped) rather than a duplicate-axiom error. A file that is still in the middle of loading (a genuine cycle: a.kurt has load "b.kurt", and b.kurt has load "a.kurt") is tracked separately and raises a clean EvalError: circular \load`: ...instead of recursing forever. The end of a loaded file closes the blocks still open in it, as a dedent does ([§7](goal-directed-proof.md), [§9](blocks-and-natural-deduction.md)): anassume/let/pick/casegives its result, asandboxis discarded -- nothing half-open leaks into your file. Aproofwhose goal isn't reached by then, or ashowwithout a proof, fails the wholeload`.

Each file is checked on its own. A loaded file is checked in a fresh context, one level deep, inside an implicit sandbox of its own (which break can't close and summary doesn't list; the main file is checked the same way): the hard-coded core (§8.1) and the files it loads itself -- nothing of the file that loads it, not its facts, declarations, or calc on. So a library can't use a fact without loading the file it comes from, and the order of two loads doesn't change what either of them proves. What the file exports (below) is then added to the loading file. A symbol that both know must mean the same there: its declarations may not contradict each other (one side may have more, e.g. number.kurt binds = of equality.kurt to the calculator), and if it is defined by a def, it must be the same def on both sides -- a def is only conservative for a new symbol, so const f / use f = 1 here and def f = 2 in the loaded file is an error. A fact that two loaded files both pass on (from a file both of them load) is added once.

A symbol is declared by one file only. The declarations of a symbol -- infix, prefix, postfix, arity, brackets, binder, flat, sym -- come from the one file that declares it; Kurt remembers which (it travels with the exports). If two different files declare the same symbol, they can't be loaded together, in either order, directly or through other files:

EvalError: `+` is declared in `number.kurt` and in `field.kurt` -- a symbol
is declared by one file only, so these two can't be loaded together

The reason: a theory's laws hold for everything written with its operators. number.kurt says $a * $b = $b * $a for every $a, $b; a theory of matrices that declares its own · or + must not get those laws. So:

  • numbers (ℕ, ℤ, ℚ, ℝ): load number (or natural, divisibility, interval, analysis, which load it);
  • linear algebra: a structure that declares its own operators, like field.kurt, vectorspace.kurt (and proofs/mafi1/matrices.kurt) -- not together with number.kurt;
  • group.kurt takes its operation as an argument (group(G, (∘), e, inv)), so it goes with either.

A theory loads what it uses. A file gets the symbols of the files that its loaded files load, too: after load natural, ∀ (from logic.kurt) and + (from number.kurt) are there. But a theory that relies on this breaks when the file in between stops loading them. So a trusted theory -- one that comes with Kurt, or one from a -p directory -- gets a note for a symbol of a theory it doesn't load itself:

; note: `forall` comes from `logic.kurt`, which this file doesn't load itself --
; `load logic` makes it independent of what the other files load

The theories that come with Kurt load everything they use (a test checks it). For a proof, this isn't noted -- load number and then = is fine -- but kurt --deps lists such symbols for any file (§1).

The same file reached twice (two files both load number.kurt) is one declaration, not two. (number.kurt used to be called arith.kurt.) In one run of Kurt, a file is checked once and its exports are reused, as long as neither it nor a file it loads changed; only the file you check itself is always checked again (it prints its steps).

The packaged theories (src/kurt/theories/), and roughly what each adds, declaring their own prerequisites via their own load lines:

theory adds depends on propositional.kurt or, not, iff, invimplies, false; aliases ⊤, ⇒, ∧, ∨, ¬; and-elim, or-intro/elim, iff-intro, iff-elim-forward/backward, not-intro/elim, bottom-intro/elim (none — builds on the hard-coded core) equality.kurt =, ≠ (a ≠ b is read as ¬(a = b), inline); equal-intro/elim propositional logic.kurt aliases ∀/∃; forall-elim, exists-intro, the rules for quantifiers with a condition (§4.4), and rewriting under a quantifier ("forall-iff", "exists-iff": from ∀ x (A ⇔ B), (∀ x A) ⇔ (∀ x B)); the quantifiers forall/exists themselves, with their roles (§8.1); unique existence ∃! x P(x) (existsunique, below) propositional, equality set.kurt the sorts of the objects (§5.2): sort set real (every number is a set; an object of no sort is any object); Zermelo-Fraenkel-style (the words of its symbols: §4.7): in/∈, ⊂ (A ⊃ B read as B ⊂ A, x ∉ A as ¬(x ∈ A): inline), ∪, ∩, separation { x ∈ A \| ... } (no unrestricted { x \| ... }, which would allow Russell's paradox; "separation-in": an element of a part of A is in A), sets by their elements {a, b} ("singleton", and generated rules, §10), ∅ (also {}), Pow, ordered pairs and tuples ((a, b), "pair-eq", fst, snd), Cartesian products A × B, mappings as sets of pairs (f ∈ (A → B): f ⊂ A × B with one pair (a, f a) for each a ∈ A), "apply", "apply-in", "function-extensionality" equality, logic, objects number.kurt arithmetic (^: "pow-two" $a ^ 2 = $a * $a for every base, the other exponent laws for a positive one); the order (<, <=; >, >= are read as them, inline); its symbols are numbers (default real); theorems proved from its rules: "squares-non-negative" (x * x >= 0), the binomial formulas "binomial-plus" ((a + b) ^ 2 = a ^ 2 + 2 * a * b + b ^ 2), "binomial-minus", "binomial-product" ((a + b) * (a - b) = a ^ 2 - b ^ 2), and "two-times" (2 * x = x + x); modal.kurt is the packaged modal theory. A modal formula is a Kurt term, not a statement, so its metavariable is $A; object connectives such as →, ∧, and □ only construct such terms. The judgment ⊢ $A, a statement, says that the term is an object-level theorem. Therefore necessitation is the ordinary Kurt schema (⊢ $A) implies (⊢ □$A), while object modus ponens has the two Kurt premises ⊢ $A and ⊢ ($A → $B). The turnstile is declared both prefix and infix: prefix ⊢ A means theoremhood, binary G ⊢ A means derivability from a represented context, and two explicit rules identify prefix theoremhood with empty ⊢ A. proofs/logic-encodings/ contains a small sequent calculus and an ordered-resource experiment without exchange, weakening, or contraction.

modal.kurt declares the optional sort formula for the formulas of modal logic, so a modal formula can't be written as a claim by itself (use □P → P is an error) -- a claim is ⊢ A, "A is a theorem". The theory still owns → and □, so it cannot be loaded together with set.kurt (where → is a function-space constructor) without future namespaces.

The former shallow theory with the same filename could not express sound necessitation because its formulas were Kurt statements: %A implies □%A also applied below an assumption. It was replaced. Moving the pretty aliases out of the minimal core lets the current modal.kurt own the paper symbols ∧, ∨, and ¬ as formula constructors without changing their role in propositional.kurt.

lambda.kurt is another deep embedding. Its type, term, index, ctx, and typing sorts reject malformed typing judgments before proof search. De Bruijn terms at zero, at (succ zero), and abs A M give complete variable, weakening, abstraction, and application rules using explicit contexts. Those judgments have the conventional surface Γ ⊢ M : A; the older prefix form has Γ M A remains available for compatibility. The theory also provides readable named terms: λ is a real Kurt binder, so alpha-equivalent terms match, and its beta rule uses sub for capture-avoiding substitution. Compatible application rules give weak beta reduction ↦; ⇝ is a deterministic left-to-right call-by-value relation with explicit values. The executable examples include a concrete preservation instance and a finite confluence diamond. General preservation and Church–Rosser need induction over encoded derivations (and a substitution lemma or parallel reduction), which the current first-order theory does not supply automatically. Pure Kurt currently expresses several sound named typing conveniences rather than the full named hypothetical-context abstraction rule; the de Bruijn representation supplies the general rule without extending the language. See tutorial/27-type-and-reduce-lambda-terms.kurt.

load with no arguments lists every file loaded so far, level by level.

docs.title: What gets exported
docs.text:
Not everything a loaded file declares becomes visible to whoever loads it. In short:

A load brings Stays in the file that wrote it its facts (use, def, proved theorems) that carry a label not marked local a fact without a label, or labelled local the symbols those facts mention, with everything known about each: fixity, arity and shape, prop places, sorts, binder, flat, sym, alias, tex, lean a symbol that only local facts mention and the file doesn't declare at its top level (its name is free again for the loader) the symbols the file declares at its top level without local (const, prop, infix, prefix, postfix, brackets, arity, binder, flat, sym, alias, chain, a sort's signature): its vocabulary a declaration with local at its end (const helper local), a declaration inside a block the symbols bound to the calculator (builtin), inline, tex and lean symbols var (a loaded var n never makes the loader's n a variable; the exported schemas arrive with internal variables) its sorts, subsorts and the sorts of the elements of its sets; its chains whose relations are all exported; its open todos the constants Kurt added at a first use (; added constant), calc on, default a def written inside a block (§6.2): it is local to the block

An exported fact that needs a symbol declared local, or a local definition, is an error when the file is loaded (drop the local, or mark the fact local too). The details:

A use/def axiom or a proved (show/proof/qed) theorem is exported exactly when it carries a label and that label isn't marked local (§6.2) — an unlabelled fact, or one labelled EXPR local "...", stays entirely inside the file that wrote it. A symbol is exported when an exported fact mentions it, or when the file declares it at its top level: a declaration written out there (const, prop, infix, prefix, postfix, brackets, arity, binder, flat, sym, chain, alias, tex, lean, a sort's signature) is the file's vocabulary. Either way, all that is known about the symbol travels along (its arity and shape, fixity, statement places, tex, lean, ...), so it can still be parsed and type-checked downstream. Not exported are: a declaration with local at its end (const helper local, prop Q, R local -- for the whole line), a declaration inside a block, var (a loaded var x would make the loader's x a variable), and the constants Kurt adds by itself at a symbol's first use (; added constant). So a symbol that only ever appears in local facts and isn't declared at the top level (or only with local) is invisible from outside, freeing up its name for something else entirely unrelated in whatever file loads this one; a symbol that an exported fact needs but that is declared local is an error (drop the local, or mark the fact local too). (Before 0.9, a declaration alone exported nothing.) A symbol bound to the calculator (builtin + add, §10) is exported too, even without a fact that mentions it: the binding is an axiom about it (1 + 1 = 2, ...) -- e.g. matrix.kurt's literals [ ], det, transpose. An alias (alias) travels automatically with whatever symbol it names, since an alias never itself appears written out in a formula — axioms are always written with the canonical name.

This makes def's two halves — the new symbol, and the fact defining what it means — travel together when exported. If a def is marked local but some other, exported fact in the same file still needs that symbol, the file fails to load with a clear error naming the symbol, rather than silently promoting the local marking away or silently leaving the symbol meaningless downstream.

The var declaration itself is file-local regardless of labelling. Before a formula is stored, however, each of its declared free variables is replaced in the formula's proof representation by a fresh internal schema variable. Its local inferred type does not occupy the printed name in the loading file. Therefore a labelled exported formula remains schematic: var p, q followed by use p and q "pq" can match A and B after load, even if the loading file uses the printed names p and q as constants. This also applies to variables in function, infix, prefix and postfix operator position. Parser-facing declarations such as arity f 1 and infix ∘ 70 70 still travel so the notation remains writable, but the variable role does not. The original expression is retained for source and normal display; generated internal names never become part of Kurt source. Normal output makes this conversion visible beside the original use as ; schema: ... (§6.2), using stable $/% names instead of the internal fresh names.

Example:

; helper.kurt
load propositional
prop P
prop Q local                     ; the declaration stays inside helper.kurt
use P            "exported"      ; travels to whoever loads helper.kurt
use Q            local "hidden"  ; stays inside helper.kurt
def R iff P      "also exported" ; R travels too, since it's labelled

; main.kurt
load helper
P                 ; fine -- P was exported
R                 ; fine -- R (and its definition) was exported
Q                 ; ProofError: can not derive `Q` -- never exported, so as far as
                  ; main.kurt is concerned `Q` is just a fresh symbol with no axiom
                  ; behind it (§3.4), not literally an "unknown symbol" error

docs.title: save: keep a shell session as a file
docs.text:
save path/to/file.kurt        ; the quotes are optional, as for `load` (needed for a name with spaces)

Writes the input lines that were accepted so far to path (relative to the current working directory): in the shell, the session without the lines that failed, and without the ones that only show something (theory, cert, help, a declaration without arguments, ...); in a file, its lines so far. The result is ordinary Kurt source, which proves its results again when it is checked, and gets its certificates in a .kurtc then (§1) -- nothing is taken over as an axiom. save needs all blocks closed and no pending show, since otherwise the saved file wouldn't load. load lines are kept as typed, so a saved file finds its theories as the session did (e.g. relative to the working directory). The name must end with .kurt and not be the name of a theory that comes with Kurt, and save works neither with --strict nor in a loaded file -- it writes the checked file's (or the shell's) own lines, nothing else.

docs.title: 7. Goal-directed proof: show / proof / qed
docs.text:
show EXPR              ; show EXPR "label"
proof
    ...
qed

show states a goal without proving it yet; it must always be followed (immediately, or after other statements) by a matching proof — proof refuses to open if there's no pending show on the current level. Inside proof, you may write any number of intermediate steps, checked exactly like top-level statements. Closing the block re-derives the shown goal from scratch, using everything true at that point (not by comparing to the block's literal last line) — so a block whose last explicit line looks unrelated to the goal can still close successfully, as long as the goal happens to already be derivable by then. If the goal can't be (re-)derived, the block does not close: a ProofError at the show (where an editor marks it), saying where the proof ends and what is missing -- the proof of `A and C` (line 4) ends at line 7 without reaching its goal -- can not derive `C`, whether qed or a dedent closed it.

qed is optional: dedenting alone already closes a proof block the same way (§9 covers dedent-based closing in general). Writing qed additionally checks that you really are closing a proof and not some other kind of block, and documents where the proof ends; either way, qed must line up with the indentation of the proof/show it's closing — dedenting is how Kurt knows how many nested blocks to close, and a single qed can close several at once this way. This is identical in a file and in the interactive shell — see §9's introduction. The end of a file closes the blocks still open like a dedent; a proof whose goal isn't reached there is a ProofError at its show. A qed that isn't written is shown as a derived line right after the last line of the proof (qed ; 7a by or-intro(7); in an editor, at that line).

docs.title: 11. Known gaps (so you don't mistake them for bugs in your proof)
docs.text:
• Derivation is single-hop (§6.1) — chain several A implies B facts manually, one derived line at a time. The one partial exception: two facts using operators from the same declared chain (§4.6) combine automatically in one step ($a < $b + $b < $c → $a < $c, etc., including implies/iff chains) — but that's still exactly one combination, not arbitrary-length automatic chaining.
  • and-elim needs load propositional (or a manual axiom instance) — it is not hard-coded the way and-intro is (§8.1).
  • A custom brackets pair does not disappear the way ( ) does — it stays a real operator, printed as e.g. []/{} in s-expression form (§4.2).

docs.title: 11.1 Not implemented, maybe never
docs.text:
Features that were considered and left out, at least until after 1.0 -- some on purpose:

  • calc that solves (§10): matching $b / 3 against 0 while $b is still unknown, or a rewrite and a calculation in one step (x = 6 from x = 2 * y and y = 3). On purpose: each line is one step a reader can check; write the step in between (x = 2 * 3, then x = 6).
  • def by pattern matching on constructors: constructors Nat 0, s (Nat is built freely from 0 and s: every element is 0 or s n, s n ≠ 0, s injective), then def fact 0 = 1 and def fact (s $n) = (s $n) * fact $n -- a recursive definition that is a definition, not an axiom. It would need the patterns to be constructors only, not to overlap, and the recursion to be structural (otherwise def f (s $n) = f (s $n) + 1 gives 0 = 1), and constructors is itself a claim about Nat (to be proven, or allowed only in trusted theories). Until then, recursive definitions are use axioms with a label (like "factorial-step" in number.kurt).
  • A normalizer for ring expressions (like Lean's ring): a line "by ring" holding if both sides are equal as polynomials, e.g. the ad - bc computations of 2×2 determinants in one line. It would need a declaration of which operators form a commutative ring and a large piece of trusted code, and a reader couldn't check such a line by one rule -- the same reason as for calc that solves. Instead: each rearrangement is a line, with the laws of the theory (proofs/mafi1/ does so); missing laws, like $a - ($b - $c) = $a - $b + $c, belong into the theory.

  • calc/eval that unfolds a user's own recursive function: print the value of e.g. fact(3) by repeatedly applying a function's own axioms (fact-zero, fact-step in number.kurt) until none apply, instead of only folding the small set of built-in arithmetic operations calc on already folds. On purpose, for now: those built-ins are hand-coded, trusted, and provably terminating; a user's recursive axioms carry no termination or confluence check, so an automatic "reduce until done" loop over them is a different, riskier kind of automation -- it could loop forever on a badly-stated recursion, and printing a trusted answer instead of a checked proof would break the rule that every claim gets a reason the kernel can check (doc/kurt-soundness.md). Until constructors and structural recursion (above) make def fact a real definition, write the unfolding as an explicit one-step-at-a-time chain instead.

  • Sort parameters (deferred, 2026-10-20): a structure over a carrier of a sort of its own, e.g. the integers as a group, group(Int, (+), 0, (-)). group.kurt's rules are over all objects ($a ∈ $G), and + takes numbers, so the instance doesn't fit the sorts. The operator could bring the sort along (polymorphic elements $$a, the sort of the use fixed by +), but group.kurt is full of $a ∈ $G, which a polymorphic variable may not be in (extensionality over the numbers alone would give ∅ = {∅}), and its definitions would have to be families, one per sort: real sort parameters for defs and rules, with a soundness argument of their own. Until a course needs it: a file about the integers as a group states the group facts it needs for + itself (dev/todo.md 40).

  • Two substitutions in one formula (not wanted, 2026-10-20): sub $x $T (sub $y $N M) is refused, and so is a sub in a goal. The search finds the value and the hole of a sub from the goal (sub_solutions), for one hole; two would make the matching higher-order unification. Only "the substitutions commute" needs it, for an older proof strategy -- preservation and Church-Rosser by parallel reduction need one sub per step (doc/kurt-current-limits.md §2.3).
  • A rule with a hypothetical premise for Kurt's own binder (not wanted, 2026-10-20): the typing rule of a named λ, has (extendx Γ x A) M B ⇒ has Γ (λ x M) (fun A B), is accepted but can't be used -- x is the binder of λ x M and an ordinary argument in the premise, and when the binder matches the goal's name, the other occurrence keeps the rule's own. Making it work would let the goal's bound name leave its binder, free in the premise -- the area of capture and eigen variables where the worst soundness bugs were -- and it would need a freshness condition Kurt can't state. The de Bruijn presentation of lambda.kurt has the general rule without the problem.
  • A second quantifier symbol for let (not wanted, 2026-10-20): let closes a block with the one universal quantifier, pick opens one from the one existential. The sort of a binder distinguishes the ranges already (∀ X over sets, ∀ n over numbers; second order as let X ∈ ℘(Obj)); a second symbol would be a second spelling, and its dispatch by sort would enter the kernel's block rules. A different display is notation (tex, inline).

docs.title: 11.2 Why no namespaces (yet)
docs.text:
Two theories loading symbols with the same name can't collide the way import does in most languages: "a symbol is declared by one file only" (§8.2) -- load number, field simply can't both declare +. Where you would expect to need a namespace -- group.kurt, field.kurt, vectorspace.kurt each wanting their own +/∘ -- Kurt uses an operator variable instead: their theorems are stated over a schematic $op (var ∘, infix ∘), instantiated at a concrete operator as an argument (group(R, (+), 0, (-)), tutorial/24), not as a qualified name. "Which +" is something you pass in, not something you look up.

The one real collision in the bundled theories is ⊢: modal.kurt's "A is a theorem" and lambda.kurt's typing judgment Γ ⊢ M : A are genuinely unrelated notations that happen to share a glyph, and only matter if one file loads both. A general lexically-scoped namespace ("open a block, use a theory's notation inside it, close it, the notation is gone") sounds like the fix, and the infrastructure for it already exists: KnowledgeBase is a stack of levels, and a declaration (infix, binder, arity, ...) is visible only from the level that made it and its descendants -- a lookup (is_infix, is_binder, ...) walks up parent, never sideways or down.

But there's a catch that makes this harder than it looks. When a block closes and one of its formulas escapes to the surviving level (assume's "impl-intro", let's "forall-intro", ...), any notation that formula needs travels with it -- the declaration is promoted to the surviving level, the same way a load's exported facts carry the notation they need (§8.2); otherwise the surviving formula couldn't be printed or re-parsed. But that also means the declaration is no longer scoped to the block once anything escapes using it: Kurt tracks every symbol "used in a formula" (parent-chain aware, like the lookups above) and permanently refuses to redeclare it differently anywhere reachable from that point on (EvalError: symbol \...` has been already used in a formula, declaring it now would change what that formula means`) -- on purpose, since silently changing what an existing fact means would be unsound. So "open a namespace, use conflicting notation, close it, reuse the symbol differently later" does not actually work today if anything inside the block survives it: the two meanings would need to be two different symbols internally, not two lexical scopes of the same one.

The smaller fix that's actually in scope is not a general namespace system, but a load-site rename for the rare real collision, so the common case stays exactly as readable as it is now and only the colliding pair needs one explicit line -- see dev/todo.md #21.

Since a grammar declaration inside assume/case/let/pick/proof was never actually scoped to the block for the reason above, it is now rejected there outright (§4.1, §6.2), the same way use/load/chain/inline already were (a def is allowed in a block since 2026-10-27: its symbol is a constant of the block, gone when it closes, and no result may mention it -- so nothing of it escapes, §6.2): infix, prefix, postfix, brackets, arity, binder, flat, sym, alias and sort must be declared at the top level, or inside a sandbox/expect whose content is discarded anyway. This closes the one case that used to look like it worked (nothing escaped the block in the test files that tried it) but was never actually safe in general.

docs.title: 2. Lexical structure
docs.text:
Kurt reads a proof one statement at a time; a statement occupies one or more physical lines (see §2.1 on indentation/continuation).

  • Comments and labels are two different things, with two syntaxes. A comment starts with ; and runs to the end of the line; Kurt ignores it completely. A ; inside a string is part of the string ("x;y" is a label), and a lean "label" TACTIC line has no comment (it takes the rest of its line raw, ; too). A line with nothing but a comment is skipped like a blank line, whatever its indentation (§2.1). A label is a string written after a fact: use A implies B "mp", show A implies C "ac", Q "derived-q" (a bare claim), def ... "name". It names the fact in Kurt's output (; by mp(3) instead of ; by 2(3)), in error messages and in --foundation, and a label that isn't marked local exports the fact to a file that loads this one (§6.1, §6.2, §8.2). A comment never labels: use A implies B ; mp is an unlabelled fact.
  • Symbols (identifiers) are [A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9]*, optionally followed by primes (a', f'') and preceded by $, % or $$ (variables, see §3.2). A Greek letter followed by digits or primes is one symbol too (λ1, ε'), also as a variable ($Γ, %φ, $Γ2). Plain multi-character identifiers remain ASCII; Greek letters next to each other (αβ) are individual symbols.
  • Numbers are INT ([0-9]+) or FLOAT ([0-9]+\.[0-9]+) literals.
  • Strings are "..." (no escaping of embedded quotes); used for labels (use ... "my-label") and for some keyword arguments that take an operator symbol as text (infix "+" 20 20).
  • Operator characters. Besides letters/digits, (, ), {, }, [, ], and , are always their own single-character symbols — they never glue to each other or to anything else, precisely so a custom brackets pair keeps working next to unrelated punctuation with no space (e.g. a trailing ...} is two tokens, ... then }, not one token that swallows the closing brace). A run of characters from .:=+-*/#&^'∈!<>|_~ (note: no brackets in this class) glues together into one symbol instead (so declaring != gives you a single two-character operator, but writing !! without spaces is one symbol !!, not two ! tokens).
