A fixed set of additional Unicode symbols is recognised one character at a time — exactly the symbols that appear as values in Kurt's LaTeX-input table (§2.2): the common logic/set-theory symbols (∀ ∃ ∧ ∨ ⇒ ⇐ ⇔ ¬ ⊤ ⊥ ∈ ∉ ∋ ⊂ ⊆ ⊃ ⊇ ∩ ∪ ∖ ∁ ∅ ≡ ∘ ↦ ⇝ → ⊢ ∞ ≤ ≥ ≠ × · ∣ ⟨ ⟩ ⟂ ∼ ≈ ≺ ≼), modal-logic symbols (□ ◇), and the Greek alphabet; ∃! and ⁻¹ are one symbol each. Any other non-ASCII character is a lexing error — you cannot declare an operator using an arbitrary Unicode symbol that isn't already on this list.
  • load (and list, tex, lean) are special in the lexer. A line starting with load (case insensitive) is scanned specially: everything after it up to a ; or end of line is taken as a comma-separated list of filenames (quoted or bare), not parsed as an expression. This is why load propositional, equality and load "my-theory.kurt" both work, without propositional/equality/"my-theory.kurt" needing to be otherwise-valid symbols. tex SYMBOL ... and lean SYMBOL ... take the rest of the line raw, as LaTeX or Lean text (§1, documents and Lean), up to a comment; lean "label" ... (a line of a proof in Lean) takes all of it, ; too -- such a line has no comment.

docs.title: 2.1 Statements, indentation, and line continuation
docs.text:
A statement can span more than one physical line: if a line ends mid-expression, Kurt automatically treats the next line as its continuation — no explicit continuation marker is needed.

In a file, indentation is significant, and the same in the shell (§9). The rule:

  • The indentation of a line is the number of its leading spaces. A tab moves to the next multiple of four (a tab stop every four columns, Python's expandtabs(4)): ⇥ and ␣␣⇥ are both 4, ␣␣␣␣⇥ and ⇥⇥ both
  • There is no option or environment variable for this, and none for the width of a block; -r N (§1) sets only the column of the reasons in Kurt's output.
  • A block opens with proof, assume, case, let, pick, sandbox or expect (§7, §9): the next line must be indented more than the opening line -- by any number of spaces (2, 4, 7, ...; Kurt's own output and the shell use 4) -- and that indentation is the block's: every further line of the block has exactly it. A line indented less closes blocks until its indentation is that of an enclosing block, and it must hit one exactly ("does not match any previous block"). A line indented more without a block opening before it is an error ("unexpected increased indentation"), except for the continuation lines of a chain (§4.6).
  • A blank line, or a line with nothing but a comment, is always safe anywhere, at any indentation, including deep inside a nested block: it's skipped outright rather than measured, so it never closes a block on its own. A comment at the end of a line (assume A ; the premise, qed ; done) changes nothing either.
  • A statement continued over several lines (a line that ends inside brackets or after an operator, use (A implies then B)) is read as one: the indentation of its continuation lines doesn't matter, and a blank or comment line inside it is skipped.

(proofs/debug/indentation-widths-and-tabs.kurt; the errors in proofs/errors/layout.kurt.)

docs.title: 2.2 LaTeX-style input shortcuts (interactive shell only)
docs.text: Typing Unicode symbols is inconvenient on most keyboards, so in the interactive shell, before a line is scanned, Kurt rewrites LaTeX-style commands to their Unicode equivalent: orall → ∀, \exists → ∃, \implies → ⇒, \invimplies → ⇐, \and/\or/ ot (or eg)/\iff/\equiv/ op/ ottom → ∧/∨/¬/⇔/≡/⊤/⊥, \in/ otin/\subset/\subseteq/ \supset/\supseteq/\cup/\cap/\emptyset/ o/\mapsto/\leadsto/\circ, imes/\cdot/\mid/\langle/ angle/\infty, \leq/\geq/ eq, ox/ /\diamond/\d (modal logic), \vdash → ⊢, and the full Greek alphabet (\alpha, \Gamma, ...). The standard LaTeX names work too: \le/\ge/ e, \lnot, \land/\wedge, \lor/\vee, \Rightarrow, \Leftrightarrow, ot. This replacement only happens for lines typed at the interactive prompt — it is not applied when reading a .kurt file. A saved proof file must already contain the real Unicode characters, or the ASCII words: every symbol of Kurt's theories has one (union for ∪, §4.7), and a file's own symbol gets one with alias.

docs.title: 1. Running Kurt
docs.text:
kurt                        # start the interactive shell (a REPL)
kurt path/to/proof.kurt     # check a proof file, then exit
kurt -i path/to/proof.kurt  # check the file, then drop into the shell (after an error: at the failing line)
kurt -d path/to/proof.kurt  # also print debug information
kurt -v                     # show the version (also `-V`, `--version`)
kurt -p DIR path/to/proof.kurt   # also search DIR for `load`ed theories
kurt -s path/to/proof.kurt       # strict, for grading (see below)
kurt -a path/to/proof.kurt       # all errors, not only the first (also `--all-errors`, see below)
kurt --budget 10 path/to/proof.kurt  # at most 10 s of search per line (see below; by default no limit)
kurt --profile path/to/proof.kurt    # after the check: the slowest lines, with their time and search steps
kurt -r N path/to/proof.kurt     # set the comment/reason column to N (default 42)
kurt --no-kurtc path/to/proof.kurt   # neither write nor use `.kurtc` files (see below)
kurt path/to/proof.kurtc             # the certificates of proof.kurt, readable (see below)
kurt --deps path/to/proof.kurt       # the files it loads, and their certificates (see below)
kurt --json path/to/proof.kurt       # the result as JSON, for graders and editors (see below)
kurt --unused path/to/proof.kurt     # check, then name the lines of the proofs that nothing cites (see below)
kurt --foundation path/to/proof.kurt # check, then show what each of its facts rests on: axioms, definitions, todos (see below)
kurt --foundation gauss proof.kurt   # ... only for the fact "gauss" (or at a line: --foundation 12)
kurt --latex path/to/proof.kurt      # the checked file as a document, proof.tex (also --markdown: proof.md; see below)
kurt --lean path/to/proof.kurt       # ... as a Lean 4 file, proof.lean (a prototype; see below)
kurt --lean proof.kurt -o -          # -o FILE: to FILE instead, -o -: to the standard output
kurt --no-line-numbers proof.kurt    # the output without the source line numbers in front
kurt --share path/to/proof.kurt      # the playground link of the proof (its text in the link; see below)
kurt --unshare LINK > proof.kurt     # the proof of such a link, back (see below)
kurt --lsp                           # a language server for editors (see below)

In the browser: the playground, www.kurt-lang.org, runs the same Kurt, checked as you type, with the tutorial, the keyword lessons, the exercises, the theories and the proofs of a lecture in its menus. A link can open one of these files: https://www.kurt-lang.org/#file= followed by its path in the playground, e.g. #file=exercises/01-knights-and-knaves/2-two-islanders.kurt, #file=tutorial/02-prove-an-implication.kurt or #file=theories/set.kurt; it shows the file's current version, and an exercise loads its scene. "Copy link to this proof" (in the menu File) gives such a link for a file opened from a menu, as long as it is unchanged; for an edited one, the link contains the text itself.

If no filename is given, Kurt starts the shell directly. If a filename is given without -i, Kurt checks the whole file, prints Proof checked (or, if any todos are left, Proof almost checked: N todos. plus a list of where they are) and exits with code 1 if checking the file raised an error (0 otherwise) — so a script (CI, an autograder) can tell a failed check from a successful one without scraping stderr text. Leftover todos still exit 0 (a todo is a deliberate, self-reported placeholder, not a failure), and errors raised only while typing at an interactive shell session don't affect the exit code either.

All errors (-a/--all-errors): by default, a check stops at the first error. With -a, it goes on after an error in the checked file, so it finds all errors that don't depend on each other; each is printed when it is found, the lines after it get their reasons as usual, and the file ends with Proof not checked: N errors. (exit code 1). To go on, Kurt does internally what a student would do to get past the error -- the file isn't changed:

  • a formula that can't be derived is admitted, as todo would (so the lines that use it don't fail because of it);
  • a block that doesn't close -- a proof whose goal isn't reached, also at the end of the file -- is closed anyway, and its claim counts as admitted (any other block is discarded, as break does); the line that closed it is then checked on its own;
  • a claim without a proof counts as admitted;
  • any other line (one that can't be read, a wrong use of a keyword, a type error) is dropped, as in the shell; if it opens a block, the block is skipped too, and so is the proof of a show that can't be read. A dropped line may cause later errors (e.g. a def that failed).

The admitted lines are errors, not todos: they aren't listed as todos, the file gets no .kurtc, and the result is failed. Some errors still stop the check: an error in a file it loads (and on a load line), anything inside an expect block (there the error is the expected result; §9.6), and a KernelError. The editors (kurt --lsp) and the playground show all errors by default; from Python, kurt.RunConfig(all_errors=True), and CheckResult.errors lists them (error is the first one).

Where a proof is slow (--profile): kurt --profile proof.kurt checks the file as usual and then prints, on stderr, its ten slowest lines with the time and the search steps of each (the load line has the time of the files it loads, cached files cost nothing):

the slowest lines of proof.kurt (1.37 s in all, seconds and search steps):
    0.85 s        0 steps      1  load logic, number
    0.40 s     1200 steps     14  x + y = y + x

From Python, kurt.RunConfig(profile=True) fills CheckResult.profile (also in --json): a record file, line, seconds, steps for each line. The editors (kurt --lsp) mark a line that took 2 s or more with an Information diagnostic (slow line: 2.4 s, 5300 search steps) and write the time into the hint at its end. An editor that asks for it (the initialization option heat: VS Code's kurt.heat.enabled) also gets two notifications: kurt/progress (the line being checked, at most ten times a second, for tinting the lines done and the line at work) and kurt/profile (time and steps of each line, after the check, for a heat map of the lines). kurt/cancel (with uri) from the editor stops the check that runs, at its next step (the editor is told by kurt/progress with done and cancelled); VS Code's status item shows Kurt: checking 12/84 and a menu with the cancel.

Budgets (--budget SECONDS), and cancelling a check: the search for one line normally takes a fraction of a second, but a false claim among many facts can take minutes (the search tries every combination before it gives up). A budget stops it: kurt --budget 10 proof.kurt allows each line 10 s of search; a line that takes longer fails with a ResourceError:

ResourceError: the search for this line stopped after 10 s, its budget -- the line is
neither proved nor refuted; a larger budget may decide it (...)

It is a kind of its own, apart from a ProofError (a rejection): the budget says nothing about the line, only that the search didn't finish. A budget never changes which steps are accepted -- it only stops the search early -- and the kernel isn't involved. With --all-errors, the check goes on after it as after a ProofError (the line is admitted, see above); expect can't name ResourceError (as it can't name KernelError), so a proof file can't depend on a budget, and an expect "ProofError" whose line runs out of budget is an error, not confirmed. The command line has no budget unless --budget says so; the editors (kurt --lsp) allow 30 s per line (the initialization option budget, 0 for none), the playground the same, and scripts/grade_exercise.py too (--budget SECONDS). The budget applies to every line checked, also in the files a proof loads.

From Python: kurt.RunConfig(time_limit=10) (seconds), kurt.RunConfig(step_limit=5000) (steps of the search: a goal against one fact, or a premise against the facts -- about 1000 to 4000 a second, the same on every machine), or both; CheckResult.exhausted says that a line's budget was used up (its errors entry has the kind ResourceError), and so does the JSON of --json. kurt.RunConfig(cancel=f) asks f() at every step and every line, and stops the check with a ResourceError at the current line when it returns true (CheckResult.cancelled; the lines after it are not checked, also with all_errors) -- e.g. cancel=event.is_set for a threading.Event another thread sets. The language server uses it to stop the check of a text that was edited meanwhile (before, the check of the new text waited for it), and the client's $/cancelRequest; an embedder of the server sets LanguageServer.cancel = f to stop its check the same way (the playground: f reads a flag in a SharedArrayBuffer that its Cancel button sets, so its worker, busy with the check, needn't be killed).

Progress, from Python: kurt.RunConfig(progress=f) calls f with a dict when a file starts, at each of its statements and when it is done: file, line (of lines), index of files (the files checked so far -- a theory that the session has checked before and that didn't change is not checked again) and done. The playground shows it as a progress bar.

Strict mode (-s/--strict), for grading: the checked file (and any file it loads that isn't trusted) may not contain use or todo, a chain there needs its rules proved before it (§4.6), and every symbol must be declared before its use (§3.2), and calc may not bind symbols to the calculator — everything has to be proven from the theories that come with Kurt, or from the ones found in a -p DIR directory (e.g. an exercise's axioms, as given by the teacher). Those are the trusted theory files; use inside a sandbox or expect stays allowed, since their content is discarded. It is a command-line switch rather than a statement in the file, so that the file being graded can't switch it off.

Certificates of a file (.kurtc): after a file checks completely (no error, no todo), Kurt writes foo.kurtc next to foo.kurt (if the directory is writable) -- the certificates of its claims (§6.5), in JSON, with the hash of the file and the files it loads. When foo.kurt is checked or loaded again, unchanged, each claim first tries its stored certificate: rebuilt with the facts as they are now (a step of the line itself that it cites, 17a, from its own stored certificate first), and checked by the kernel; only if that doesn't work, Kurt searches as usual. So the output is the same, it is just faster (for the proof files of this repository, up to five times). A .kurtc can't make Kurt accept anything the kernel doesn't check -- a wrong or outdated one only costs the time of the search -- so it is also used with --strict. Kurt writes and uses .kurtc files when run as kurt (the command line or shell); from Python, only in a session with kurt.RunConfig(kurtc=True) -- for a text (check_text), only for the files it loads, not for the text itself. kurt --strict foo.kurtc checks foo.kurt with the same options as kurt --strict foo.kurt.

The theories that come with Kurt come with their certificates: the package has them next to the theories, and the single-file kurt.py embeds them (scripts/build_certificates.py makes them). In them, a theory of Kurt is named <kurt>/propositional.kurt, not by where it is, so they fit wherever Kurt is installed. If a theory's directory isn't writable, its new certificates go to the cache directory ($XDG_CACHE_HOME/kurt, or ~/.cache/kurt). A .kurtc that is up to date isn't written again. (Without them, load divisibility in the single-file kurt.py took 8 s each time, 1.2 s with them.)

kurt --json foo.kurt checks the file and prints the result as JSON (exit code as above): ok, complete (also no todo left), error, error_kind, error_line, failure (why a step failed, §6.1), errors (each with its kind, line, column, message, failure, and the file for an error in a file it loads; with --all-errors all of them, else the one), exhausted and cancelled (a budget was used up, the check was cancelled; see above), todos, loaded (the files it loaded, also through other files), certificates (of each line, as cert shows them), the text output, and events, each printed line as a record -- the source line, its id (5, 5a, 11-13), its kind (step, claim, open, close, assumed, load, declaration, expect, error, text, other), level, text, the rule and the lines it uses, its label, the user's comment, and where they apply its steps and schema:

{"line": 5, "id": "5", "kind": "step", "level": 0, "text": "B", "reason": "5 by rule(4)",
 "comment": "modus ponens", "rule": "rule", "uses": ["4"]}

From Python, the same comes from kurt.check_file(path) or kurt.check_text(text) (a CheckResult, with .events and .to_json()). A text is never trusted (under strict, it may not use), whatever name it is given -- trust comes from where a file is read. One exception, for the editors: a text under the path of a theory of the running Kurt that is exactly that file's text (saved, unchanged) is that theory, trusted like it; a changed text is not. Like the command line, the module refuses to check under python -O (which removes Kurt's internal checks).

Does the file prove a given theorem? ok and complete say that the file checks (an empty file is complete), not what it proves. result.proves(statement, label=None) says whether the file proves statement at its top level: derived in this file by steps that rest on no admission -- not a use or def, not a todo or a claim whose proof contains one (anywhere in the proof, needed or not) or uses a fact that was admitted (a todo F before it, a claim admitted after an error with --all-errors), not a fact of a loaded file, not a claim that is withdrawn (break) or only proved inside a block. With label (or a label written in the statement, proves('A ⇒ B "ab"')), the fact must carry that label; without one, any label will do. The statement is written as Kurt reads it, with or without show, and is read in the file's final context: A ⇒ B and A implies B are the same statement, A ∧ B and B ∧ A too (∧ is sym), and a statement the file can't read (a notation it doesn't declare) is one it doesn't prove. result.proof_of(statement, label=None) says how the file states it: 'proved', 'admitted' (a todo, or a proof that rests on one or on an error), 'assumed' (use, def), 'loaded' (a fact of a file it loads, not proved here), or None (not stated at the top level); when it is stated more than once, the best counts. result.loaded lists the files the check loaded, directly or through other files, by their paths -- a grader checks it against the files a solution may load (scripts/grade_exercise.py: only what the exercise loads; a file that states the answer is no proof, even if the solution derives the answer from it in one step). Neither says anything after a check that stopped at an error (proves is false, loaded empty); with all_errors, the check runs to the end, and proves tells the claims whose proofs are sound from the ones admitted after an error.

>>> result = kurt.check_text('load propositional\nprop A, B\nshow A ∧ B ⇒ A "a"\nproof\n    assume A ∧ B\n        A\nqed\n')
>>> result.proves('(A and B) implies A'), result.proves('A ∧ B ⇒ A', 'b'), result.proof_of('A')
(True, False, None)

A proof as a link (--share, --unshare). The playground's Share button makes a link that holds the whole proof: https://www.kurt-lang.org/#proof=CODE, where CODE is the text of the file as UTF-8 bytes in base64 with - and _ instead of + and /, without the = padding (no compression, nothing secret: anyone can read it; an optional &folder=tutorial/ after it says where the proof's loads find their files). kurt --share foo.kurt prints that link for a file (it doesn't check it), and kurt --unshare LINK prints the proof of a link, or of the bare CODE, so that kurt --unshare LINK > foo.kurt gives a file to check. A very long proof makes a link that browsers and chat programs may cut (a few thousand characters): for a file that the playground has, #file=exercises/01-knights-and-knaves/2-two-islanders.kurt is short. The same without Kurt, in Python:

import base64
def share(text):                  # the link of a proof
    return 'https://www.kurt-lang.org/#proof=' + base64.urlsafe_b64encode(text.encode('utf-8')).decode().rstrip('=')
def unshare(link):                # the proof of a link
    code = link.split('#proof=')[-1].split('&')[0]
    return base64.urlsafe_b64decode(code + '=' * (-len(code) % 4)).decode('utf-8')

or in a shell, python3 -c "import sys,base64; print('https://www.kurt-lang.org/#proof=' + base64.urlsafe_b64encode(open(sys.argv[1],'rb').read()).decode().rstrip('='))" foo.kurt. (In the library: kurt.kurt.share_link(text) and unshare_text(link), which also gives the folder.)

What a fact rests on (--foundation). kurt --foundation foo.kurt checks the file and then shows, for each fact at its top level, its class -- axiom (use), definition (def), todo, or theorem (a proved line, or a show with its proof) -- and, for a theorem, what it rests on: the use axioms and defs that the steps of its proof cite, directly or through the facts they cite, by file; the todos that admit a step; the steps computed by the calculator (calc on), with the symbols' bindings and the file whose builtin made them (`+` add, `=` eq of number.kurt). A fact without a label is named by its line (line 12), with its statement in its own heading: an unlabelled use is an axiom of the file like a labelled one (only it isn't exported). Found by walking the certificates of the steps (§6.5): through the blocks (a block's result rests on what its last line rests on; the block's own assumption is discharged when it closes, so it is no postulate), and into the theories it loads (a loaded theorem brings what it rests on in its file). A theorem with no todo behind it is established, relative to these axioms and definitions; one with a todo (or, with --all-errors, a line admitted after an error) is accepted relative to it. The class of a fact stays what it is (§6.3.1): use is an axiom, also where it could be proved. After the facts, the reverse: each postulate with the facts that rest on it -- for a change of an axiom, this is who is affected. For a teacher choosing a trusted set of theories: which uses a theorem really needs. kurt --foundation LABEL foo.kurt (or kurt foo.kurt --foundation LABEL) shows one fact, found by its label or its line: a theorem with what it rests on, an axiom, definition or todo with the facts of the file resting on it. In an editor (kurt --lsp), the hover of a theorem at the top level says it in one line: "rests on: 2 axioms of gauss.kurt, 3 axioms of natural.kurt, 1 def, the calculator, no todo".

gauss.kurt: what each fact at its top level rests on

"gauss" (line 12, theorem): established, relative to 4 axioms, 1 definition and the calculator
    gauss.kurt: "sum-def" (line 5), line 14 computed by the calculator (`+` add, `=` eq of number.kurt)
    natural.kurt: "induction" (line 40), "plus-zero" (line 22), ...
    equality.kurt: "equal-elim" (line 23)

each postulate, and the facts above that rest on it:
    ...

The rules a chain declaration stands for appear as the rules of `chain = < <=`. From Python, check_file(path, foundation=True) (and check_text) fills CheckResult.foundations, one record per fact -- label, line, file, text, class, status (established/accepted, or the class of an axiom, definition or todo) and rests_on, each postulate with its kind (use, def, todo, calc, admitted), file, line, label and text (and for calc, bound_in: the files of its bindings) -- and result.foundation("gauss") finds one by its label (or line); kurt --json includes them as foundations. Nothing is stored for this: it is computed from the certificates after the check, so it costs nothing where it isn't asked for.

kurt --lsp is a language server (the Language Server Protocol, over stdin/stdout) for editors -- VS Code (the extension of kurt-syntax), Emacs (Eglot), and Neovim. A file is checked when it is opened and saved. A client can request debounced checks while typing. Errors and todos appear as diagnostics at their lines, the reason of each checked line appears at its end (an inlay hint) and on hover; what a line prints besides a reason (builtin, infix, theory without arguments, cert 14, ...) appears on hover too (its first 60 lines); a line without a certificate says on hover what it does, with its own symbols (var a, b: "a, b stand for anything ..."; infix ^ 75 74: right-associative; calc on, tex, ...); a theorem at the top level says what it rests on ("rests on: 3 axioms of propositional.kurt, 1 def, no todo", see --foundation). A line inside a proof that nothing cites is greyed out (a hint with the LSP tag "unnecessary", as an unused import), and kurt --unused names these lines: backwards from what must stay -- the top-level lines, the labelled ones, qed, and a proof's last line that is its goal -- along what each step cites; a block's result cites the block's last line and its first, so a block whose result nothing needs is greyed out entirely. A line that restates a block's result (∀ x Q(x) after a let block), an assumption, or the line before it isn't greyed out: it helps the reader, and the hover says that Kurt doesn't need it. Only lines of proof, assume, let, pick and case blocks are reported, and only of a file without errors; "nothing cites it" isn't "it could be deleted" (a step may be found without citing a line that helped). And completion knows the state at the cursor (the next step, the value after = with calc on, LaTeX shortcuts, theories, and names). Positions use the LSP's UTF-16 convention, so mathematical symbols before a completion or hint do not shift it.

The initialization options are theoryPaths (additional trusted theory directories), strict, allErrors (all errors of a file, the default; false: only the first, as kurt without -a), budget (seconds of search per line, 30 by default; 0 for none; a line that takes longer gets a ResourceError diagnostic, see "Budgets" above), checkOnChange (also accepted as checkOnType), and checkOnChangeDelay in seconds. A check of a text that is edited while it runs stops at its next step. The directory of the edited file is searched first but remains untrusted; only an explicit theory path grants trust. When an open document loads another open document, Kurt checks the current unsaved text of the loaded document. Closing a document clears its diagnostics.

kurt --deps foo.kurt shows the tree of the files that foo.kurt loads (read from their load lines, before anything is checked), each with the state of its certificates and the dates of the file and its .kurtc:

gauss.kurt  -- certified  (file 2026-09-29 06:11, certificates 2026-09-29 06:13)
└─ analysis.kurt  -- certified  (file 2026-09-28 16:11, certificates 2026-09-29 06:13)
   └─ natural.kurt  -- out of date: the file changed since  (file 2026-09-29 07:02)
      ├─ set.kurt  -- certified, but logic.kurt changed since  (...)
      ...

"certified, but ... changed since" means: the certificates fit the file, but a file it loads has changed -- they are still tried (and checked by the kernel) the next time, and rewritten after it.

After the tree, --deps checks foo.kurt (quietly) and lists the symbols it uses from theories that it doesn't load itself, by theory -- e.g. logic.kurt: `forall` for a file that loads only natural and writes ∀ (see load, §8.2).

The .kurt file is the only source of truth. Everything else is derived from it, can be deleted, and is never trusted: a .kurtc only holds hints, which the kernel checks each time; the reasons Kurt prints and cert only show a check that already happened; and save writes Kurt source again, not a snapshot of facts.

kurt foo.kurtc shows the certificates of foo.kurt, line by line, as cert does: the goal, the rule (with its file and line), the values of its variables, and the facts it uses, and the blocks it closes. Kurt checks foo.kurt for that (quietly, with the .kurtc), so what is shown was checked by the kernel; the first line says whether the .kurtc still belongs to the file.

Documents and Lean (--latex, --markdown, --lean, -o). A checked proof as a document: kurt --latex proof.kurt writes proof.tex, kurt --markdown proof.kurt writes proof.md -- each line in mathematical notation, indented by its block, with its reason, and then the certificates. A line that continues a chain is written as in mathematics, its relation and its right side (= x), without the left side Kurt repeats. How a symbol is written comes from its theory:

tex alpha \alpha                    ; a symbol
tex sum \sum_{$1=$2}^{$3} $4        ; $1, $2, ... the places of the arguments, in the order of
                                    ; the shape (`arity sum _ (_, _) _`: the variable, a, b, T)

(only output: nothing Kurt checks changes; exported with load). The tex lines, and the lean lines (below), belong in the theory files, with the symbols they write -- not in a file of their own (decided 2026-10-23); Kurt's theories in src/kurt/theories/ keep theirs there. Without a declaration, Greek letters and symbols are written by their LaTeX names, longer names upright (\mathrm{abs}), and a variable $x as x -- as \mathsf{x} only where a constant x is in the same formula.

A Lean 4 file of a checked proof (a prototype): kurt --lean proof.kurt writes proof.lean (it doesn't run Lean; the last line Kurt prints is the command for that), and lean proof.lean checks it again with Lean's kernel. It writes each step from its certificate -- the rule with the certificate's values, and its premise from the cited facts -- and the theories' rules as Lean axioms (but those with a proof in Lean, see below), so Lean checks the proof, not the theories. Kurt's objects are one type Obj, its statements Prop; a flat or sym operator comes with its associativity or commutativity as an axiom (that is what the declaration asserts), ∀ x ∈ A P is ∀ x, x ∈ A → P and ∃ x ∈ A P is ∃ x, x ∈ A ∧ P (§4.4's "forall-cond-def"/"exists-cond-def"), any other binder is a constant applied to fun x => ... (sum i (a, b) T is sum a b (fun i => T); logic.kurt's ∃! x P(x) is what its definition says, ∃ x, P x ∧ ∀ y, P y → y = x, by its lean), a def is a Lean def with its defining equation proved by rfl (a def inside a block an obtain ⟨t, h⟩ : ∃ t, t = R := ⟨R, rfl⟩ in the proof, local as in Kurt; a def over a tuple, def coprime($a, $b) ⇔ ..., a function of the components, coprime a b; the defs of the symbols in what a step cites of a loaded file are Lean defs too), a case step rcases, and a symbol that is applied and also an object (f a, f ∈ (A → B)) is an Obj applied with k_apply. Without a number theory, a number is a constant of its own (k_num_17 : Obj; 0 and 1 of field.kurt are its zero and one, which only its axioms describe -- Kurt knows nothing else of them there), and a calc step is not translated: a sorry, listed at the end of the file. The rules of propositional.kurt, logic.kurt and equality.kurt are theorems of Lean's logic (each lean "label" grind, see below; invimplies by its lean), so Lean checks the logical rules a proof uses, with or without Mathlib.

With Mathlib (numbers). A theory says how its symbols read in Lean (with Mathlib, but for propositional.kurt's lean invimplies ($2 → $1) and logic.kurt's ∃!), as tex does for LaTeX (raw to the end of the line, $1, $2, ... the places of the arguments; one template per number of arguments, so - has two; only output, exported with load):

lean Obj ZFSet                      ; the Lean type of Kurt's objects (set.kurt)
lean real ℝ                          ; the Lean type of the sort `real` (number.kurt), embedded into it
lean complex ^ k_cpow $1 $2          ; the `complex` profile of the overloaded `^` (complex.kurt)
lean + $1 + $2
lean - $1 - $2                      ; `a - b`
lean - -$1                          ; `- a`
lean - opaque $1                    ; `- a` has no Lean meaning here: a constant of its own
lean ! Real.Gamma ($1 + 1)
lean Nat member $1 ∈ Set.range (fun n : ℕ => (n : ℝ))     ; what `x ∈ Nat` means
lean {_,...,_} k_numset (fun x_ => ∃ k_ : ℕ, x_ = $1 + k_ ∧ x_ ≤ $2)   ; a set with `...`, by its shape
lean lim (Filter.limUnder (nhdsWithin $1 {$1}ᶜ) $2)        ; a binder: `lim v a T`

A lean declaration replaces the one of a file it loads (for the same number of arguments). An overloaded operator (§5.2) is written by the least sort of each occurrence: lean SORT OP TEMPLATE for the profile of that sort, else the operator's own lean (+ of ℝ or of ℂ: Lean's + either way), its arguments cast to the profile's type. A binder's places are its condition (if it has one) and its body, both as functions (fun x => ...), and the arguments between them, a range (a, b) as two (sum i (a, b) T: $1 a, $2 b, $3 the body). member declares a set of numbers: a definition, the set of the embedded numbers with the property (k_numset), and what membership in it means a theorem (k_mem_Nat : ∀ x : ℝ, k_emb x ∈ Nat ↔ x ∈ Set.range ...) -- from it the rules about the set are theorems. A set written with ... has the lean of its shape, {_,...,_} for {a, ..., c}, {_,_,...} for {a, b, ...} (the places are its elements).

A model of a theory's own operations. lean SYMBOL def TEMPLATE makes the template a Lean definition (@[irreducible] noncomputable def, named by the symbol and the number of arguments), and the terms use its name -- they stay small, and the laws of a flat/sym operator are proved by unfolding it. A numeral can be mapped like a symbol (lean 0 ...) where no theory of numbers gives it a type. field.kurt is the example: K is the set of the embedded reals, and the operations decode their arguments (k_dec, the inverse of k_emb), compute in ℝ and embed the result:

lean K def ZFSet.range (fun x : ℝ => k_emb x)
lean 0 k_emb (0 : ℝ)
lean + def k_emb ((k_dec $1 : ℝ) + (k_dec $2 : ℝ))

modal.kurt has a model of its own as the objects (lean Obj ((Nat → Nat → Prop) → Nat → Prop), Kripke semantics): kurt --lean field.kurt and kurt --lean modal.kurt prove every axiom of the theory true in its model (doc/kurt-soundness.md §11).

Sets and numbers. Kurt's objects are the sets of Mathlib's model of ZFC (ZFSet, set.kurt's lean Obj ZFSet), and a sort with a type of its own -- number.kurt's lean real ℝ -- is embedded into them, as real ⊂ set says: k_emb : ℝ → Obj is a definition (an ordinal for each real, by a well-ordering, and its von Neumann level), injective by Mathlib's theorems, so nothing is assumed. A variable, constant or binder of the sort real is a real (∀ x ∈ Nat over ℝ, x a number by its places or default real), every other object a set; a number at the place of a set is k_emb x (1 ∈ A is k_emb 1 ∈ A, {1, 2} Lean's own {k_emb 1, k_emb 2}, (1, c) the Kuratowski pair ZFSet.pair), and = between a number and a set compares them as sets. In set.kurt ∈ is ZFSet's membership, ∅, ∪, Pow, ×, A → B (ZFSet.funs) Mathlib's, {z ∈ A | P} separation (ZFSet.sep; a part chosen among the numbers, {n ∈ Nat | n > 2}, with the property read on the embedded numbers, k_lift), a mapping applied, f a, the b with (a, b) ∈ f (k_apply, a choice), and every rule of set.kurt, its theorems and the rules of a set by its elements ($x ∈ {a, b, c} ≡ ...) are theorems of Mathlib. So a proof that mixes sets and numbers is checked against one model of both -- no axiom of set.kurt is read over the reals. The rules of propositional.kurt, logic.kurt and equality.kurt are proved once for every type (∀ {α : Type u}: their variables without a sort), so "forall-elim" applies to ∀ x ∈ Nat over the reals and to ∀ x over the sets alike. Without set.kurt and the numbers (field.kurt, group.kurt, vectorspace.kurt: no sorts), the objects stay an opaque Obj.

The theories of numbers all read Kurt's numbers as Mathlib's reals ℝ (number.kurt's lean real ℝ; Real, Int, Rat of number.kurt and natural.kurt's Nat extend it, as in Kurt): Nat, Int, Rat are the sets of the embedded casts of ℕ, ℤ, ℚ, so - and / are the real ones everywhere, ^ is the real power Real.rpow, and n! is Γ(n + 1) (Real.Gamma: 0! = 1 and n! = n (n - 1)! for every n > 0, the two rules number.kurt has, and the factorial for a natural number). In analysis.kurt abs is |x|, sum i (a, b) T the sum of T(b), T(b-1), ..., T(b - k) for the k + 1 = ⌊b - a⌋ + 1 terms that are at least a, and 0 for a > b (the empty sum: "sum-empty"; "sum-last" is for a <= b + 1), max/sup the supremum sSup of the values (min/inf: sInf), argmax a choice (Hilbert's ε), lim and tends Mathlib's limit along the punctured neighbourhoods; in continuity.kurt and derivative.kurt cont, diff, deriv are ContinuousAt, DifferentiableAt, deriv; in sequences.kurt converges and seqlim the limit along atTop of the values at 0, 1, 2, ...; in integral.kurt integral is Mathlib's interval integral and integrable is read as "continuous on [a, b]" (the rules make a function integrable only that way).

complex.kurt reads complex as Mathlib's ℂ (lean complex ℂ): a real where a complex number is required is its cast ((x : ℝ) : ℂ), z + x is the + of ℂ and x + 1 of reals the one of ℝ, i is Complex.I, re, im, conj, cabs are Complex.re, Complex.im, starRingEnd ℂ, ‖z‖. Among the sets a real is the complex number it is: k_embC embeds a complex number with imaginary part 0 as its real part (k_emb), every other one at a von Neumann level above those of the reals (a definition, injective, nothing assumed), and Complex is the set of them. The complex ^ is k_cpow, the real power on two reals (^ is one function: a real power is a complex one) and Mathlib's cpow otherwise. A rule about complex numbers used for reals (complex-div-self for x / x = 1) is a statement about their casts, which Mathlib's casts bring back (norm_cast, push_cast).

The theories' rules are theorems. A rule's proof in Lean is kept with the rule, in its theory:

use $a = $b  ⇒  $a + $c = $b + $c   "add-eq"
lean "add-eq" intros; subst_vars; rfl

lean "label" TACTIC is a line of a proof (a tactic, raw to the end of the line, ; too, so no comment after it; more lines for the same label are the next lines of the proof, an indentation after one space is kept) of the fact "label" of the file, at its top level and after the fact -- only output, as tex: Kurt doesn't read the tactic. kurt --lean writes such a rule as a theorem with this proof instead of an axiom (with a comment -- number.kurt:70 "add-eq": proved in Lean), so Lean checks the theory's rules, not only the steps of the proof; a tactic that doesn't prove the rule is an error in Lean. The rules a chain of Mathlib's relations generates (chain = <= <: "chain-trans-1-2") are theorems by linarith, as flat/sym of + are by ring, and what the calculator knows of Nat (6 ∈ Nat, k_calc_Nat) is one of k_mem_Nat; a def of a loaded file that a step uses is a Lean def, as the file's own. Every rule of the theories of numbers (number, natural, divisibility, analysis, continuity, sequences, derivative, integral) and of set.kurt is proved this way -- interval.kurt's six rules of {a, ..., c} and {a, b, ...} too (the sets of their shapes' lean) -- but "integral-riemann" (true for a continuous function, but its proof isn't in Mathlib); and the theorems Kurt proves in number.kurt, natural.kurt and divisibility.kurt have a lean "label" too, for a proof that cites them (those about ⊂, even, odd, ∣, coprime unfold the defs of these symbols). The tactics don't name the variables (intros, ‹_›): Kurt orders the arguments of +, * and ∧ its own way, and names its variables by numbers. kurt --lean number.kurt writes a theory itself, all its rules with their proofs.

Where the proof's theories give a lean Obj, kurt --lean writes import Mathlib, abbrev Obj : Type 1 := ZFSet.{0} with the embedding instead of the opaque axiom Obj : Type, a number 2 as (2 : ℝ), a mapped symbol by its template (the others stay axioms), the laws of a mapped flat/sym operator as theorems (ring), and a calc step by norm_num (then simp, ring_nf, linarith, decide; for a fact that computes to the goal, the same on the fact and the goal) -- what none of them closes stays a sorry, which Lean reports. The last line Kurt prints is then lake env lean FILE, to run in a lake project with Mathlib. Kurt's repository has one, scripts/lean (Lean and Mathlib of the same version as scripts/lean-toolchain; neither Kurt nor pip install kurt-lang needs it):

cd scripts/lean && lake exe cache get      # once: Mathlib's prebuilt files, ~5 GB in scripts/lean/.lake
python3 scripts/lean_check.py proof.lean   # Lean with Mathlib if the file imports it, else plain `lean`

-o FILE writes the document (or the Lean file) to FILE instead of next to the proof, -o - to the standard output, for a pipe: kurt --lean proof.kurt -o - | lean --stdin, kurt --markdown proof.kurt -o - | pandoc -o proof.pdf. Then what Kurt says goes to the standard error, and a proof that doesn't check writes nothing (an error, exit status 1). With -o, one format per run (without it, --latex --lean writes both files).

docs.title: 10. Session toggles and output
docs.text:
format sexpr | normal | source     ; stored tree, readable normal form, or source spelling
hint on | off                  ; in the shell: before each prompt, what could come next
calc on | off       ; a step may follow by computing with numbers (the symbols bound with `builtin`)

Each, called with no argument, reports its current setting instead of changing it (format also names the other options).

format normal is the default readable form and reflects Kurt's stored normal form; format sexpr exposes the exact expression tree. format source replays the input spelling saved on a stored formula (aliases, parentheses and operand order included); an expression that was generated internally and has no independent source spelling uses normal formatting. Editors should use structured API/LSP data when they need positions rather than parsing any display.

What calc computes is said by the theories: they bind their symbols to Kurt's built-in calculator, whose operations are add, subtract, negate, multiply, divide, power and the comparisons eq, ne, lt, le, gt, ge. number.kurt does

builtin + add, - subtract, - negate, * multiply, / divide, ^ power
builtin = eq, < lt, <= le

(>, >= and ≠ are read as <, <= and ¬(… = …), inline §6.2; the negation of a computed comparison holds by calc, ¬(2 = 3))

and a symbol that isn't bound is never computed. Sets of numbers, too: the calculator knows naturals, integers and rationals, natural.kurt does builtin Nat naturals (number.kurt likewise for Int and Rat), and set.kurt builtin in element; then calc on proves 3 ∈ Nat and -3 ∈ Int, but not -3 ∈ Nat. complex.kurt binds i to imaginary: an expression of numbers, i and the operations is computed exactly with rational real and imaginary parts, calc on proves (1 + 2 * i) * (3 - i) = 5 + 5 * i, i * i = -1, (1 + i) ^ 2 = 2 * i (a power with a natural-number exponent up to 64) and i ≠ 0.

builtin gives a symbol a meaning that Kurt itself implements: a calculator operation, as above, or a role of the engine. The engine gives no symbol a meaning by its name alone -- only the roles that the theories assign:

role in what the engine does with it equivalence propositional.kurt: builtin iff equivalence a fact A iff B is used as A implies B and as B implies A; def may define with it disjunction propositional.kurt: builtin or disjunction case blocks for the alternatives of a fact A or B or ... close by "case-elim" (with propositional's "or-elim") negation, falsum propositional.kurt: builtin not negation, false falsum an assume A block whose last line is false also gives not A ("not-intro") equality equality.kurt: builtin = equality def may define with it universal, existential logic.kurt: builtin forall universal, exists existential the outer ∀s of a fact are stripped (its variables stand for anything), let closes with the universal ("forall-intro"), pick opens from the existential ("exists-elim"); they need a binder with two arguments setbrackets, setbuilder, emptyset set.kurt: builtin { } setbrackets, \| setbuilder, builtin emptyset emptyset (∅) sets by their elements and by a property: see below

A role needs the matching prop signature (prop iff 0 1 2), a role has one symbol, and only a trusted theory -- one that comes with Kurt, or one from a -p directory -- can assign a role, since it changes what the engine derives (a calculator operation, like an axiom, also in other files, but not with --strict). So a file's own iff or or, without propositional.kurt, is just a relation.

Sets (set.kurt, since 0.9): with the roles of sets, braces make three kinds of terms -- {a, b, c} by its elements (({} a b c)), {x ∈ A | P} by a property (the set-builder, the | term itself; | outside braces is an error), and {}, which is ∅. So a rule about {$y}, like set.kurt's "singleton" ($x ∈ {$y} ≡ $x = $y), never reads a set-builder or a list as its one element (before, it proved false, proofs/soundness/sets-by-their-elements.kurt), and {(a, b)} is the set with one element, the pair. For each set by its elements in a line, Kurt adds the rules for it to the file (from the source <set enumeration>, checked by the kernel like any rule): each element is one, c ∈ {a, b, c, d} in one step ("element-3-of-4"), and membership is the disjunction, $x ∈ {a, b, c} ≡ $x = a ∨ $x = b ∨ $x = c ("enumeration"), which case splits -- for a set of constants of the file this rule is of the set itself, otherwise of its length ("enumeration-n"). The order of the elements counts for the terms, {a, b} = {b, a} follows from "extensionality". About 15 elements take a second or two; a disjunction of twenty or more is slow to find (dev/todo.md, speed).

With interval.kurt, ... lists numbers: {a, ..., c} in steps of one ("range"), {a, b, ..., c} and {a, b, ...} in steps of b - a, for a < b ("progression", "progression-intro", "progression-infinite", ...) -- each membership is an ∃ k ∈ Nat (proofs/natural-numbers/progressions.kurt). One or two elements fix the step; more, as in {2, 3, 5, 7, 11, ...}, would only suggest a pattern, which Kurt can't know, so it refuses them: write a set-builder, {p ∈ Nat | prime p}.

The set-builder is one construct with three parts: the variable x, the set A it ranges over, and the statement F -- "the set of the x in A with F". Kurt writes it with two pieces of syntax, the braces and the binder | (it has no operators of three pieces), and reads it as one term: the braces are dropped (set_terms), and the | node remains with two arguments, the binding condition x ∈ A (the variable and its set together, as in ∀ x ∈ A F) and the body F. So the variable is bound like by any binder (§4.4), the body is a statement (§5.1), and x ranges over the elements of A. Without a set, {x | F} is refused: unrestricted comprehension would allow Russell's paradox (set.kurt's "separation" only carves a part out of a given set).

Vectors and matrices (matrix.kurt, load matrix): a bracket pair bound to matrixbrackets (builtin [ ] matrixbrackets, both brackets of a pair declared with brackets [ ]; a bracket pair takes no other role) makes literals of numbers -- [1, 2, 3] a row, [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]] a 2x3 matrix row by row, [[1], [3], [5]] a column (a row [1, 2, 3] and the one-row matrix [[1, 2, 3]] are the same value) -- and the operations add, subtract, negate, multiply (a number times a matrix, or a matrix times a matrix), transpose, determinant and the comparisons eq, ne compute them exactly (/ divides numbers only). Shapes that don't fit give no value. Written over several lines, each line inside the brackets is a row, as on paper:

A = [1, 2, 3
     4, 5, 6]          ; is [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]

In normal screen output, a matrix with two or more rows is printed on aligned lines, while row vectors stay compact:

[[  1, 20],
 [300,  4]]

This is display only. Saved .kurt source keeps the accepted input lines, and format sexpr keeps its one-line structural representation. format source shows the spelling originally entered for a stored formula.

(a line break inside a bracket pair bound to matrixbrackets -- builtin [ ] matrixbrackets -- without another one in it ends a row; elsewhere it is a space, also inside a [ ] that isn't bound: the theory makes the brackets special, not Kurt). matrix.kurt has its own +, -, ·, so it isn't loaded together with number.kurt (§8.2); it computes with literals and has no laws for matrices written with variables (for those: proofs/mafi1/matrices.kurt, over a field). As everywhere with calc on, a name defined as a matrix (def A = ...) isn't computed in the same line: replace it first, one step per line.

A binding is like an axiom (1 + 1 = 2, 2 + 1 = 3, ...), so --strict rejects it outside the trusted theories, and the symbols of a trusted theory can't be bound anew. Numbers bound to calculator operations are constants: the binding supplies fixed semantics and reports const SYMBOL ; added constant if that role was not already known. A variable or binding operator cannot also be calculator-bound. Numbers are exact: integers, decimals (0.1 is exactly one tenth, so 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3 holds), and fractions, which stay fractions (1 / 3 + 1 / 3 is 2 / 3). What has no exact value isn't computed: 1 / 0, 0 ^ -1, 2 ^ 0.5, and 0 ^ 0 (which number.kurt leaves open). Neither is a result with more than 1000 digits, and a longer number literal is a ScanError. 0 + x and 1 * x are x, 0 * x is 0. In number.kurt, ^ is right-associative and binds more tightly than the prefix -: - 2 ^ 2 is - 4, and 2 ^ 3 ^ 2 is 2 ^ 9. A decimal with an integer value is that integer: 1.0 is 1.

With calc on, a line may follow by computing -- it is not changed: it is stored as written. It follows if its computed form follows (e.g. 1 + 1 = 2 is computed to 2 = 2, by calc), searched with the computed forms of the facts written with calc on -- or, if not, as written (so (1 + n) * (1 + n) = 1 * (1 + n) + n * (1 + n) is an instance of "distrib-add", and from 7 = 1 + 6 follows ∃ k (7 = 1 + k)). No symbolic simplification. A comparison of numbers (e.g. 3 <= 4, 2 + 2 < 5) is proven directly "by calc", and a claim follows "by calc" from a fact that computes to the same thing (e.g. x = -25 from x = (-5) * 5). (Before 0.9 each line was computed when it was read.) Results of substitutions (sub, as in induction or equal-elim) are computed too: substituting k + 1 into $x + 1 gives k + 2, not k + 1 + 1. While matching a rule, a part of it is computed as soon as its variables have values: with $n := 3, the ($n - 1)! of "factorial-step" matches 2!, and after def f($x) = $x * $x, f(3) = 9 follows in one step. But calc doesn't solve: the $b / $c of "gt-div-pos" doesn't match 0 while $b is still unknown -- state such steps as their own lines, or use a rule that fits (like "div-pos"). Nor does it combine a rewrite with a calculation: x = 6 doesn't follow in one step from x = 2 * y and y = 3 -- write x = 2 * 3 in between, then x = 6 follows by calc. Not implemented on purpose: solving for an unknown while matching, or several steps at once, doesn't fit the idea that each line is one step a reader can check (§6.1); the line in between is the step. calc on holds for its block and the blocks in it, and ends with it (and with its file): after the qed of a proof that switched it on, it is off again (before 0.9 it stayed on). With hint on, the shell prints before each prompt what could come next (; hint: next, e.g. proof): proof after a show, in a proof its goal and then qed, in a chain its relation, in a case block the other alternatives -- Tab on an empty line writes it.

breakpoint, a line in a proof file: at a terminal (or with kurt -i FILE), checking stops there and the shell continues with that state -- the open blocks, the facts, what is still to prove; try steps there, then write the one that works into the file (Ctrl-D ends the shell). Without a terminal (the playground, Kurt from Python), it shows that state and checking goes on. In a file that another one loads, it is skipped. After an error, kurt -i FILE likewise continues in the shell at the failing line, with the state there (keywords/42-breakpoint.kurt).

Tab in the shell (at a terminal) completes: on an empty line the next step (as hint); after = with calc on the value (17*42= and Tab gives 17*42=714); a LaTeX shortcut its symbol (\forall and Tab gives ∀); after load a theory or a .kurt file here; otherwise keywords, symbols and labels ("and- gives "and-elim"). With several possibilities, Tab writes what they have in common, and a second Tab lists them. It only writes text; every line is checked as usual.

help prints Kurt's own one-line description of every keyword, help use the one of use.

docs.title: 5.1 Statements and terms: prop
docs.text:
Kurt has two categories of expressions: statements, what is proved, assumed and combined with ∧ ∨ ¬ ⇒ ⇔ ∀ ∃, and terms, the objects -- any and the sorts below it (§5.2), which form a DAG (field ⊂ ring and field ⊂ ordered is fine; where two sorts meet, the meet must be one sort). prop declares which places take statements:

prop P, Q              ; P and Q are statements (propositional constants)
prop even 0            ; `even n` is a statement: the result place 0
prop ∧ 0 1 2           ; `∧` takes two statements and is one
prop = 0               ; `a = b` is a statement; its places 1 and 2 are terms

Position 0 is the result, 1, 2, ... the arguments; prop P is short for prop P 0. Every place is a statement place or a term place: a place prop doesn't name is a term place.

A statement is no object (decided 2026-10-20): a statement at a term place is a type error -- c = (A ∧ B), A ∈ M, f(A ∨ B) -- and so is a term at a statement place. Statements are compared with ⇔, not =. This is what the search and the kernel always did (no step puts a statement in for a term variable), and what the Lean export says (statements are Prop, terms Obj). Truth values as objects (a function into {true, false}, a Boolean algebra) are terms of a sort of their own (sort truth), never statements.

prop is no sort: sort prop and sort any prop are refused, sort doesn't list it, no term fits a statement place.

Statement variables. %A is a statement variable, by its sigil -- as $x is a term variable: in propositional logic, the propositional variable; in a rule of first-order logic it may contain the rule's term variables (∀ $x %A with sub $x $t %A). var p with prop p is the same with a plain name (§3.2). A statement variable is schematic: free in a use or a show, it says "for every statement" -- use false implies %A, show %A ∨ ¬%A -- and the search puts any statement in for it. Binders range over terms (decided 2026-10-20): ∀ p (p ∨ ¬p) with a statement p, and ∀ %A ..., are type errors -- nothing is lost, the schema says the same, and no file needed a statement bound inside a formula (proofs/soundness/binders-range-over-terms.kurt). So let, the introduction of ∀, fixes a term only: a proof about %A needs no let -- the claim's %A is one statement throughout the proof, an assume holds it fixed (proofs/soundness/let-fixes-a-term.kurt).

First use. A new operator applied to statements gets those places at its first use, and that is final, like the first sorted use of §5.2 (infix xor 20 20, then A xor B: xor takes two statements, c xor d with terms is then a type error); a new constant used as a statement becomes one. Kurt prints the declaration it inferred, for example prop P 0 ; added statement places, next to const P ; added constant. Use explicit prop declarations where stable vocabulary and early typo detection matter; --strict additionally rejects undeclared symbols.

Only use/show/bare top-level claims are required to be statements overall (the error is "must be a statement"); a binder's body is what the binder says -- a statement for ∀, ∃ and {x ∈ A | F}, a term for sum.

docs.title: 5.2 Optional user sorts
docs.text:
General sorts are optional. A theory that declares none has only the two categories of §5.1, statements and terms (all of sort any).

Declare any additional categories a theory needs:

sort nat, vec
nat a, b
vec v, w

Each new sort name becomes a declaration keyword with the same positional notation as prop:

nat + 0 1 2            ; result and both arguments are natural numbers
prop < 0               ; the result is a statement
nat < 1 2              ; both arguments are natural numbers
vec · 0 2              ; vector result and second argument
nat · 1                ; natural-number first argument

A convention of the theories, not a rule of the language: sorts are lowercase, sets are capitalized. real x says what kind of thing x is (a sort, syntax); x ∈ Real is a fact about x (a set, an object a fact can be about). The number sort is real (set.kurt, real ⊂ set; Kurt computes exactly with the rationals among them), the sets of numbers are Nat, Int, Rat, Real (ℕ, ℤ, ℚ, ℝ).

All sorts are inhabited (a model has at least one object of each, doc/kurt-spec.md §2.2): a file that declares a sort and names no object of it -- no constant of the sort or of a smaller one, no numeral -- gets a warning at its end ("the sort vec ... has no constant in this file"), since it assumes one.

Position 0 is the result; positions 1, 2, ... are arguments. A symbol without positions is short for result position 0, so nat a means nat a 0. Unmentioned positions remain unconstrained. Different sorts may describe different positions of one operator, but one position cannot have two sorts. A sorted variable remains constrained when Kurt instantiates it as part of a rule, including after the rule crosses a load; proof search and the certificate kernel both check the constraint.

docs.title: Subsorts
docs.text:
An item of a sort line is one name, or a chain of names read like chain (§4.6): sort set real int declares the names that are new and makes int ⊂ real ⊂ set; commas separate items, sort set real, set vec gives set two subsorts. The relation is a DAG with its transitive closure (int ⊂ set too); a cycle is an error, also one that a load would make. The line says what it declared:

sort set real int                          ; real ⊂ set, int ⊂ real

A value of a sort fits a position or a variable of the same sort or of a bigger one: a number fits where a set is required (3 ∈ {3}), a set doesn't fit where a number is ({1, 2} + 0 is a type error). A sorted rule stays strict: a rule about the numbers never applies to a set, and one about the sets applies to a number. A sort name where a symbol is declared is refused with a hint (set real -- "a subsort is declared with sort set real"). sort alone lists the sorts and the subsorts with where they were declared.

any is the sort of all objects, every sort is below it, and every symbol without a sort is over all objects: a variable, a bound variable and a block's constant, inside a formula as at its top (∀ x (x ∈ A ⇔ x ∈ B) is about all objects wherever it is written, so it meets "extensionality"), and a constant until a use gives it a sort. set and real (set.kurt) are restrictions below any, real ⊂ set: a binder over the sets is one over fewer objects, like one over the numbers. set.kurt declares the places that are sets (set ∈ 2, set ⊂ 1 2, set ∪ 0 1 2, ...) and has no default: an element (the left of ∈, an element of {a, b}, the variable of a set-builder, a component of a pair) is any object.

A fact gives no sort: x ∈ Nat says nothing about the sort of x (sorts are syntax, facts are semantics). ∀ x ∈ Nat ranges over the numbers where x is a number by its places (x + 1) or by default real; natural.kurt's induction applies to it only then, so a proof about numbers writes default real. There, ∀ n (n ∈ A ⇔ n ∈ B) is about the numbers only and doesn't meet "extensionality"; for sets of numbers natural.kurt has "ext-real": (∀ n (n ∈ A ⇔ n ∈ B)) ∧ A ⊂ Real ∧ B ⊂ Real ⇒ A = B, with the set Real of all numbers ("real-all": every number is in it) and Nat ⊂ Real, Int ⊂ Real, Rat ⊂ Real -- rules with proofs in Lean, not a link between sorts and sets (proofs/natural-numbers/sets-of-numbers-are-equal.kurt). ℕ, ℤ, ℚ, ℝ (typed \N, \Z, \Q, \R) are aliases of Nat, Int, Rat, Real. The elements of a set written by its elements ({1, 2}, {0, 2, ...}) have the sort of the elements. A polymorphic rule writes its bound variable $$x (logic.kurt: ∀ $$x %A ⇒ sub $$x $a %A): it is used for a binder over any sort, and the checker verifies that $$x occurs only in its binder, in subs and as a side of =.

docs.title: Inference and default
docs.text:
A symbol without a declared sort takes the sort of its first sorted use, in every file: with real + 0 1 2, const x and then x + 0 = x make x a number; x ∈ A makes A a set. The line that gives a symbol its sort says so, like an inferred prop signature:

7  x + 0 = x                     ; by add-identity
   real x                         ; sort inferred

info x shows the sort and how it came (real x 0 ; level 1, f.kurt:7 (inferred)), and so does the hover of the line in an editor. = is polymorphic: it gives no sort.

Where a use also takes smaller sorts -- the left of ∈ takes any set, and a number fits -- the default of the file decides, if it fits; without one, the position's own sort (x ⊂ A: a set). The default decides only at an element (the left of ∈, an element of {a, b}), not at a set: in $a ∈ $A, $A stays a set. Before its first sorted use (x = y: = gives no sort) a symbol has none: it is any object.

The first sorted use is final. No later line changes the sort of a symbol: x ⊂ A makes x a set, and a later x + 1 is a type error, also though a number is a set. To use it as a number, declare it before its first use (real x); a number fits wherever a set is required. The message says both places and what to declare:

TypeError: `x` has the sort `set` (inferred at line 3), but here it is used as `real` -- the first
sorted use decides; to make it a `real`, declare `real x` before that use

A fact gives no sort -- b ∈ Nat doesn't make b a number -- and the message says that too, when such a fact is known. A declared sort, the sort of a defined symbol (def c = R: the sort of R), the sort of a witness (pick w with ...: the sort of the existential's variable) and that of a symbol of a loaded file are final as well.

default SORT (only after sort SORT; not prop; at the top of a file, not inside a block): from this line on, every $ variable, operator position, bound variable and new constant of this file without a declared or inferred sort gets SORT -- an operator's positions at its first use after the line, except a statement place, and a binder's variable with the binder (sum i (0, n) i: i a number). The last default counts, from its line on. It doesn't cross load, but the sorts it gave to the file's symbols do, as sorts do. default alone names the one in force. default any is the same as none: a symbol without a sort is any object anyway, and a constant gets its sort at its first sorted use. number.kurt, natural.kurt, divisibility.kurt and the analysis theories have default real; set.kurt, group.kurt, field.kurt and vectorspace.kurt have none (their symbols are over all objects). A student's file has none, unless it wants one: after default real, every symbol that has no other sort is a number. "No other sort" includes what the line itself says: in use A = {n ∈ Nat | n > 2} the other side of = is a set, so a new A is a set there, not a number (proofs/soundness/default-yields-to-equality.kurt).

Variables ($x, a var, a bound variable) get their sorts per formula, from all their places in it -- the same formula always reads the same; a constant of a block keeps the sort it got there when the block closes: let x, then x + 1 > x, gives ∀ x (...) over the numbers, also if the last line doesn't mention arithmetic (the kernel checks it, doc/kurt-kernel.md).

docs.title: A checker sort versus an object-level carrier
docs.text:
sort nat and const Nat express different design choices. A sort belongs to Kurt's checker:

sort nat
nat n

This constrains where n may occur, but nat is not a term, set, or proposition. In contrast, natural.kurt declares Nat as an object-level constant (of sort set). Together with membership from set.kurt, $n ∈ Nat is an ordinary mathematical proposition that can occur in assumptions and theorems. The two don't meet: n ∈ Nat gives n no sort, and a checker declaration real n does not prove n ∈ Nat.

A sort property does not decide whether a symbol is a constant or variable, just as prop, infix, and arity do not. Write var a or const a when the role matters; otherwise the usual first-use rule still applies. A declared sort name is reserved and cannot also be a term symbol or Kurt keyword. Sort declarations and signatures must precede the symbol's first use.

For a binding operator, the declared sort of its first position also types a fresh bound name in the body. sub x a A preserves the result sort of A; if x has a sort, its replacement a must have it. A rule of logic.kurt, written with $$x, is used for a binder of any sort (∀ x over the numbers): its bound variable stands for the binder's, and each sub checks the sort of what it puts in -- all $$ binders of one use over the same sort, and only a rule whose $$ variable occurs nowhere else but in subs, = and where it is bound; "extensionality" ($c in its body) is about all elements, and for the numbers alone it would make ∅ = {∅} (doc/kurt-soundness.md §8.41-§8.42).

docs.title: Order-sorted logic, and why it is sound
docs.text:
These sorts make Kurt an order-sorted logic: a partial order of sorts with any on top, values that fit wherever a bigger sort is required, and rules for every sort at once ($$x). What makes that sound -- every variable has a sort, substitution respects it, binders are the same only over the same sort, one sort per use of a polymorphic rule, $$x only where the sort doesn't matter, non-empty sorts, a meet for every two uses of a symbol -- and where each is enforced (by the search and again by the kernel) and tested (proofs/soundness/, Lean) is in doc/kurt-soundness.md §10. Restriction (∀ x:set P to ∀ y:real P) and widening (∃ x:real P to ∃ x:set P) are no rules: let with "forall-elim" and pick with "exists-intro" do them (proofs/restriction-and-widening.kurt).

Every top-level sort declaration crosses load as part of the theory's public vocabulary, even if no exported fact uses it yet; so do the subsorts. Sort signatures cross with the symbols that exported facts need (not those of $ variables: their sorts are in the facts), and all declarations retain their source locations. A sort is declared by one file only (set.kurt declares set and real, and number.kurt loads set.kurt). Inspect them with:

sort                     ; prop plus every user sort, and the subsorts
nat                      ; every nat signature
list sort lambda         ; sorts retained from lambda.kurt
list term lambda         ; term signatures retained from lambda.kurt

Generic equality deliberately remains polymorphic: prop = 0 constrains its result but leaves its two operands unsorted. A theory may add more specific operators when it wants stronger checking.

Overloading. An operator may have a second signature on the same places for a sort that fits the first one (real ⊂ complex): + - * / ^ of number.kurt have one on real and, after load complex, one on complex (complex.kurt). A signature is of one sort at all its places (complex ^ 0 1 2: the exponent of z ^ 2 is a complex number too), so abs : complex -> real can't be one -- complex.kurt has cabs. A term gets its least sort from its syntax: 1 + 2 and x + y for reals are real, z + 1 with a complex z is complex, so (1 + 2) < 3 is well-sorted and z < 3 a type error (< is on real). A law of the reals is not used for a complex value (z + 1 doesn't fit its real variable); complex.kurt has the same laws for complex. A new constant at a place of an overloaded operator is inferred to be the smallest sort (x + 1: a real); a complex one is declared (complex z). Only a theory of Kurt can add a signature to an operator of another file; a signature for unrelated sorts (real, vec) is not possible yet (decision 19 of dev/todo-sorts.md, stage 2); doc/kurt-kernel.md §8.5 has the soundness argument.

One table of sorts per symbol, whatever its fixity. The places in a sort line are the argument positions of the symbol: 0 for the result, 1, 2, ... for the arguments. A symbol that is both prefix and infix, like -, has one table: real - 0 1 2 (inferred in number.kurt) covers the prefix use - x (places 0 and 1) and the infix use a - b (places 0, 1 and 2). So unary and binary minus can't have different sorts for their first argument; an overload along a chain of sorts (complex - 0 1 2, doc/kurt-spec.md §2.3a) covers both. A sort line for a symbol of a theory of Kurt is refused ("it would change the meaning of -"), as are brackets and chain for it.

docs.title: 5.3 Operators are no objects; functions as values are mappings
docs.text:
An operator -- a function symbol (arity f 1), +, ∪, a predicate -- is no object: it is applied, never compared, quantified over, or passed where a term is required. f = g for two function symbols, P(f), a ∀ x instantiated with f: each is a type error ("f is an operator without its arguments -- an operator is no object; a function as a value is a mapping"). The one exception is an operator parameter, a place where a defined predicate takes an operator: group.kurt defines group($G, (∘), $e, (ι)) with the operator variables ∘ and ι, so group(R, (+), 0, (-)) passes + and - there -- a schema, which the definition unfolds into first-order formulas about + and -.

A function that is a value is a mapping of set.kurt: a set of pairs, f ∈ A → B, applied by juxtaposition, f a. Mappings are objects: they are compared (two mappings from A that agree on A are equal, "function-extensionality"), they are elements of sets, a quantifier ranges over them. Like every fact, f ∈ A → B gives f no sort; declare set f (proofs/set-theory/function-extensionality.kurt):

set f, g
use f ∈ (A → B)
use g ∈ (A → B)
use ∀ a ∈ A (f a = g a)
f ∈ (A → B) ∧ g ∈ (A → B) ∧ ∀ a ∈ A (f a = g a)
f = g                                 ; by "function-extensionality"

Why (decided 2026-10-20). Until then an operator was also a value: f = g was accepted and rewrote f c to g c, P(f) was a formula, and ∀ k included the operators. That has no first-order meaning: the soundness argument (doc/kurt-kernel.md §8) models an operator as a total function, not as an object, and in the model of the Lean export -- ZF sets -- ∪ or a field's + as an object would be the graph of an operation on all sets, a proper class. A bare operator also had the sort of its result, so with real f 0 1 the function f counted as a number (f + 0 = f was well-sorted, and a fact about all numbers applied to f). Making operators first-class objects would have meant an applicative semantics, a sort of its own for operator values and a Lean model with objects that are no sets -- higher-order logic through the back door. Kurt stays first-order: operators are applied, mappings are the functions one can talk about, and the operator parameters of structures are schemas. The search (bare_operator_for), the kernel (k_has_kind) and the type check (bare_operator_as_value, operator_parameters) agree on it.

docs.title: 5.4 Operator variables: var ∘ with infix ∘ 70 70
docs.text:
An operator is no object (§5.3), so a definition or theorem that holds for every operation -- a group, a field, "associative", "reflexive" -- can't take the operation as an argument. Kurt uses an operator variable instead: a symbol that stands for an operator, declared in two lines,

infix ∘ 70 70      ; its shape: an infix operator, as `+` is (a relation: `prop R 0`, then `var R`)
var ∘              ; ... and a variable: it may stand for any operator of that shape

(group.kurt writes infix compose 70 70, alias ∘ compose, var compose; the word is the standard name, the symbol its alias.) Its rules:

  1. In a rule, an operator variable matches an operator by itself. $a ∘ $b matches x + y and x mix y and a ∘ b, through the unifier (∘ := +), not as a hole at a term (§8.1). The properties of the operator it stands for (flat, sym) apply as usual.
  2. An operator parameter is a place where a defined predicate takes an operator. In the definition it is written in round brackets, def selfinverse($A, (∘), $e) ⇔ ..., and at a use, selfinverse(R, (mix), e), group(R, (+), 0, (-)). This is the only place where a bare operator is allowed. (- x) is still - x.
  3. A definition with an operator parameter is a schema. use selfinverse(R, (mix), e) unfolds into the first-order formula e ∈ R ∧ ∀ a ∈ R (a mix a = e) about the actual mix: no operator is ever a value, so the soundness argument stays first-order.
  4. Everything else with an operator is refused. An operator without brackets at an argument is a parse error (token + cannot start an expression), (mix) = (mix) is a type error (an operator is no object), and so is quantifying over it (∀ ∘ (x ∘ x = x)).
  5. The var stays in its file. Only the infix ∘ is exported by load, not the var: a file that loads group.kurt can use ∘ as an operation of its own (tutorial 24).
  6. It replaces namespaces (§11.2): "which +" is something you pass in, not something you look up.

Example (proofs/debug/operator-variable.kurt):

load propositional, equality, logic, set
infix ∘ 70 70
var ∘
arity selfinverse (_, _, _)
def selfinverse($A, (∘), $e) ⇔ $e ∈ $A ∧ ∀ $a ∈ $A ($a ∘ $a = $e)   "selfinverse"

infix mix 60 60                       ; a word as the operation of this file
const R, e, x
use selfinverse(R, (mix), e)
use x ∈ R
e ∈ R ∧ ∀ a ∈ R (a mix a = e)        ; "selfinverse" unfolded, with `∘ := mix`
∀ a ∈ R (a mix a = e)
x mix x = e

A relation is a parameter in the same way: prop R 0, var R, then R(x, y) (or x R y with infix R 20 20), e.g. def reflexive((R), $A) ⇔ ∀ x ∈ $A (x R x) and reflexive((<=), A).

docs.title: 3. Terms, symbols, and their roles
docs.text: Every parsed term (Expr internally) is either a single symbol/number/ string (a leaf) or an operator applied to one or more sub-terms. There is no separate "statement" syntax — a term is a formula once it's been checked to be a statement (§5).

docs.title: 3.1 Function application is just an infix operator
docs.text:
Space is a built-in infix operator (declared in the hard-coded minimal.kurt, see §8.1), so f x means "f applied to x". A symbol without an arity is curried: f x y is f x, applied to y, and (f x) y is the same term -- both are stored as one call, (f x y) (so f x is no subterm of it that a rule could rewrite). With a declared arity (§4.3), f takes exactly that many arguments, and further ones apply to the result: with arity f 2, f x y z is (f x y) z, and (f x) y is an error, f x lacks an argument -- a forgotten argument or a misplaced bracket is caught. f(x, y) is something else: f applied to one argument, the pair (x, y) (§4.3). Where a function is applied in steps as a term of its own, as in the lambda calculus, a theory writes application as an operator (lambda.kurt). This is also why you can write not A even though not is declared as a prefix operator elsewhere — a bare symbol symbol juxtaposition is space-application regardless.

Function application binds more tightly than every other operator, as in mathematics: f x + y and f(x) + y are (f x) + y, and s n in Nat is (s n) in Nat. Parentheses only group, so f(x) is just f x -- with one difference: a bracket written directly after a symbol, without a space, makes one term that binds more tightly still. So inv det(A) is inv (det A) (while inv det (A) is inv det A, inv with the two arguments det and A), and in the condition of a binder, ∀ $x ∈ Perp(M) Q($x) reads Perp(M) as one term.

docs.title: 3.2 Constants vs. variables
docs.text:
Every symbol in a formula is exactly one of (before its first use, a symbol with only a shape or type declaration, infix, arity, prop, is neither yet, §3.4):

  • a constant — one fixed, specific object, declared with const x, or implicitly whenever it's introduced by let/pick/def/brackets, or the first time a symbol that isn't a variable (no sigil, no var) is used in a formula (e.g. after use P c, both P and c are constants; prop only records the statement places of a symbol, see §5, not whether it is a constant). Such a first use is shown as an ordinary declaration in the output (const P ; added constant), including when the symbol already had a syntax or type declaration such as infix P ... or prop P. A wholly undeclared symbol is often a typo; with --strict (§1), it is an error instead. Or
  • a variable — may stand for arbitrary objects, declared with var x.

Once a symbol's role is fixed on a given level (see §9 on blocks/levels), it cannot be changed in either direction on that level: declaring const x then var x fails, and so does the reverse. A symbol that is a constant inside a block can still be an ordinary (as-yet-undecided) symbol outside it, once the block closes and its constants go out of scope.

A var needs no let in a proof. A show about declared variables is a claim for all of them, and its proof works with them as they are: no let x, y first (that is for a const-like fresh object, §9.2). After var x, y, show x > y implies not x = y is proved by assume x > y, assume x = y, ... directly (regression test: proofs/debug/var-needs-no-let.kurt).

A sort with the names. var real x, y, z declares the variables x, y, z and gives them the sort real: it is var x, y, z followed by real x, y, z (§5.2); const real c, d is const c, d and real c, d the same way. Only the plain form: a sort in front of the list, no places (real x 0 is the sort line of §5.2 itself).

How Kurt handles variables (the design, kept as it is on 2026-10-15):

  • A variable stands for anything: a use, def or todo with a variable in it is a schema, which the search instantiates by matching -- use $a = $a gives c = c for every term c. A variable is written with a sigil, $x for a term and %A for a formula -- or as a plain name declared with var x, which is the same thing in nicer clothes: the theories write var n, m and then use n + 0 = n, as a textbook would. Kurt shows the schema it reads (; schema: ∃ z (R z $x)), and warns when a use only relates declared variables (use a <= b with var a, b says every number is below every number).
  • A constant stands for one object. const c declares it; let x, pick c and def introduce one; so does the first use of an undeclared name.
  • Inside a block, a variable can be held fixed: let x (a new name, or a declared var x; let $x is a type error, a $ name is always a variable) makes it an arbitrary but fixed object for the block, and closing the block gives the ∀ (§9.2); an assumption's variables are fixed inside it the same way (assume P $x: one $x throughout the block).
  • load exports no variable: a loaded file's var n stays its own, and its schemas arrive with internal variables ($$07), so the loader's n is free for anything. A declared var of the loader can't be a constant of a loaded file, or the other way round (§7 of doc/kurt-soundness.md).
  • Variables are never a value of each other's binders: a $T under a binder over $i stands for a term that doesn't depend on $i, unless the rule only ever uses it under that binder or with a substitution for $i (sum $i ($a, $b) $T; doc/kurt-soundness.md §8.10).
